COBALT, Ont, July 14.-Every passing
hour adds to the list of those dead, in
jured and rendered destitute in the fire.
devastated Porcupine district, where the
property loss probably is more than
S2,OOOOOO.


The number of dead in the district
remains largely a matter Of conjecture
About ninety bodies either have been
buried or designated for shipment in the
collins now being rushed northward by
the carload. Many persons are missing
from the more densely populated town.
ships


How many of the hundreds living In
comparative Isolation have perished only
days of work by the organized relief
parties can reveal. A message from
Porcupine early today stated that seven
bodies had just been found at the Vipond
mine. Their condition made identifica-
ton impossible.


Flocking to the Towns.


Men, women and children, thinly clad
and bearing marks of the awful fight
against flames and smothering smoke, are
still flocking into the larger towns in
this vicinity and at North Bay. Those
escaping with slight injuries or none
have gone through to North Bay, to be
carried free of charge by the Canadian
Pacific railroad and Grand Trunk rail
way to their destinations.


Those less severely injured are taken
to hospitals in Haileybury, Cobalt, Liske-
ard and North Bay. All these hospitals
are filled with sufferers.


Hundreds of people are at Porcupine
awaiting special trains out. About 1000
already have left.


Farmers Abandon Homes.


SELLWOOD, Ont, July 14-Serious
bush fires have been raging for three
days along the Canadian Northern rail-
road from Sudbury to Sellwood. Mil
lions of feet of timber have been de-
stroyed and farmers, with their families,
have abandoned their homes.


Many fed toward Sudbury. Along the
railway they found several bridges burn
ed away. The fire at one time reached
the outskirts of Sudbury and threatened
It's destruction.


The total loss here is about $3.50 OOO.
No loss of life has been reported.


Narrowing Tales by Refugees.


NORTH BAY, Ontario, July 14-Hun-
dreds of refugees are coming out of Por-
cupine on special and regular trains, and
all tell narrowing stories of terrific fights
for life. Many bodies are reported strewn
along the trail.


At the Big Dome mine a splendid fire.
fighting apparatus was available, with
powerful pumps and plenty of hose, but
nothing could withstand the flames. Two
hundred and sixty men were working at
this mine, and it is thought that all
except ten escaped. When the fire struck
the Big Dome men ran in all directions.
some went down the shaft, others ran
toward the lake.


The man fell exhausted in deep ditch,
and by Keeping his face covered with mud
for three hours managed to save his life
Those who went down the shaft were
suffocated. as the shafthouse and even
the timbering of the shaft walls was
burned Six bodies have been recovered
from the Big Dome shaft, and twenty
seven bodies have been recovered at West
Dome.


Reports from South Porcupine grow in
horror one survivor states that twenty
two people were swept off a raft on Por-
cuplne lake in the storm.


Hundreds of people stood for five hours
in the water. where the only breath avail
able was close to the waters surface
between waves, which dashed spray over
water. and the first search brought out
nine bodies from Porcupine lake.


Twenty or More Drowned.


Estimates of the number drowned range
from twenty upward.


Seven bodies We're found on the trail
between Hollinger and McIntye mines,
half mile apart, and five bodies have
been found on the Vipon property.


Relief trains with provisions. tents and
blankets are, being rushed in over the
government railway. and the food supply
at Porcupine is now adequate.


Hundreds are coming out Of the fire
zone. and North Bay is crowded with
refugees awaiting trains to their former
homes.


The Night Hawk district also was
caught by the flames, and several deaths
there are reported. Many are coming
out with bandaged arms and heads suffer-
ing from severe burns and all tell Of a
fearful death roll and many injured.


Days will pass before anything like
accurate estimates Of the dead can be
made.

New York, Dec. A.-Clean breaks are
the rule hereafter for boxing bouts in
New York State. Since the new State
law controlling the sport went into eff
feet last spring there has been some
confusion regarding breaks, some ref
erees allowing boxers to hit with one
hand free.


At its weekly meeting the State boxing
commission settled the matter, and to
enforce the rule provided that referees
negligent in this respect may be brought
before the commission. The commission
also decided that in future a boxer can
have only four seconds in his corner, and
that seconds must stay in the corner
where they belong.

There have been four Official cele-
brations of the Fourth in Washington.
This years is called the third safe and
sane Fourth because 1t was not until
1908 that the institution was regarded as
being permanently established.


The first official celebration was in
1903. 1t was not altogether a success
1t indicated the growth Of the people
wish that the greatest day in their his
tory should be less noisy and dangerous,
but the response to the sentiment was
not general. The Commissioners of the
District, who inaugurated the move
ment, were forced to believe that the
safe and sane Fourth was something
that could not then be had.


Opening District Building.


The idea was set aside for five years.
The Commissioners in 1905 got up an
other official celebration and connected
it with the opening of the District
building. 1t was a great success. They
got the building open with due formal
ity and ceremony, had a celebration OF
Independence Day that delighted the
people of the District, and established
the fact that for celebrative purposes
noise and fire and smoke were prac-
tically things of the past except when
used in an orderly and esthetic man
ner. They proved that the things for
celebration are properly modutated
sounds and artistically arranged colors,
and words of patriotic cheer and hope.


The Commissioners made the safe and
sane Fourth permanent institution IN
the following year. They prohibited the
salF and use of fireworks in the Dis
trict by any person other than duly au-
thorized committees representing public
celebrations.


First "No Damage" Celebration.


A committee, which, changing in per-
scnnel without changing in authority
and purpose, has acted in succeeding
years, was appointed, and 1t successfully
consummated a complete program for
the Fourth in 1909. For the first time
there were no disasters to life and prop
erty resultant from the celebration of
the Fourth.


The 1909 celebration comprised the
same features of the 1910 celebration,
and the same as those planned for
Tuesday. There were band concerts
and the setting off of fireworks by duly
appointed agents and numerous athletic
events. The 1910 celebration was even
better than the preceding one. 1t
again saved life and property, and
again gave pleasure to the people


The Commissioners and the commit
tee believe they have good auguries for
Tuesday, they said today.

cruelty is almost unbelievable.

national guard at home, are active

Inhabitants Of Chichen Itza were hold
ing their remarkable ball tournaments
after the fashion OF the ancient Greeks
who celebrated the Olympic games with
something of religious fervor as well as
out of love for sportsmanlike contests.
The Chichen Itzaites gathered for their
ball games much as did the ancient Ro-
mans for their gladiatorial combats, for
frequently victory was celebrated. by
human sacrifice = the victims being
thrown into the sacred wells OF the Itza
after a very elaborate ceremony Of con-
secration. On other occasions the con-
testants wagered their own liberty on
their prowess.


The game was played with a rubber
ball. which. as the ancient chroniclers
explained with ingenious accuracy, IVES
made from white drops which exude
from a certain tropical tree, but which
become hard and black when exposed
to the air for several days" The balls
were large and solid. the eighteen-inch
aperture being barely large enough to
allow them to pass through with ease.


The two enormous stone rings were
fixed in the side walls near the top. %
or Is feet in the air. The contestants
sometimes nine or ten on a side, but
more frequently playing singles-were
not allowed to touch the balls with their
hands, but were supposed to make the
strokes with the point Of the hip, which
was covered with rawhide.

Mrs. Latham.-Gather large and small
! cucumbers when cool and dry and with


the stems and flowers on them. Put IN
stone jar with salt and water and


cover with grape or cabbage leaves.
Set them where they will keep warm,


but not actually cook, for fortnight,


until they turn quite yellow. Then re-
move the leaves and drain water and


salt from them. Then place them in a


bell metal or copper kettle with the salt
| and water drained from them; cover
again with leaves and set over the fire


until they turn green.


When very green and clear take them
off and drain from the water and salt,
changing twice a day for two days.


Then dry with cloth. split open length
| wise and scrape out the seeds. Have


ready a thin sirup made OF a quarter


of pound OF sugar to a pint of wafer


and two ounces of whole ginger. Let It


get cold: then pour over the cucumbers.


Turn of the sirup and reheat and pour
over the cucumbers twice every day for


three or four days. Let it get perfectly
cold: then tie up and put away.

Dissatisfied with the decision of Judge
CaIlan, in refusing to grant her the Gus
tody of her little daughter, Mary Partee,
of 13 Naylor court northwest, created a
scene in the Juvenile Court yesterday by
attempting forcibly to take the child
from her husband Noah Partee, Of 206
l. street southwest


For a number of years Mr. and Mrs.
Partee have been separated, the wife liv-
ing in Baltimore, and the husband and
daughter, Lillian, residing here. Mrs.
Partee yesterday filed petition request
ing that the daughter be committed to
the Board of Children's Guardians. on
the ground that Lillian did not have a
proper home and was not suitably cared
for. Attorney Hughes, representing Mrs.
Partee at first asked that the court
grant the woman the custody of the
child, but Judge Callan explained that
such a question was outside the jurisdic-
ton of the court


Girl Given to Father.


He then asked that the girl be taken
away from the father, declaring that
she was worked excessively, and that
her father failed to give her proper at
tention. The prosecution showed that
the girls present home is an excellent.
one, and the court refused to grant the
petition.


Partee had started out of the court
room with the girl when Mrs. Partee
rushed toward him, grabbed her daugh-

eral officers of the court rushed into

the mother. The mother waited out

grabbed her and attempted to take

neighborhood.

In the death of William Vickers Price,
soldier, writer, and actor, who was
buried several days ago. there passed
character we'll known in Washington
and one to whose life more than ordi-
nary romance was attached. Price was
born in South America, where his father
gained fame and wealth as a railroad
builder for Dom Pedro, then President
of Brazil, nearly sixty years ago.


At the height OF his fame Price senior
died, leaving William Vickers Price and
two other small children dependent upon
their mother, who also died shortly after
ward of yellow fever. The three children
were sent back to England by Dom
Pedro, where William Vickers Price was
raised by his grandfather, entering the
British army as member of the Seven
teenth Lancers and seeing service in
Africa and India.


Later he purchased his discharge, came
to America about 1880, and became a
newspaper writer for time, afterward
going on the stage with James O'Neill.
Price later entered the government serv-
ice, where he continued for years He
retired short time ago. and when he
died last Sunday was mourned by thou
sands who knew him as man OF rare
talents

IN the COS, soon after John Ericssons tur-
reted Monitor defended the Union the
ptalnsmen Of Kansas were making use on
and Of the turret idea, From Hays, at that
time the farthest point reached by the Union
Pacific, the Smoky Hill route ran for hum
dred and twenty miles west through Trego,
Cove, Logan, and Wallace Counties.


The stage ranches. where horses were
changed and drivers cared for, were much
ha1rassed by Indians. Stables were fired and
women and children were captured or killed.
The Government was unable to provide
garrisons strong enough to patrol Smoky Hill


TIC protect themselves the frontiersmen
devised and built prairie monitors. The
monitor was deep cellar, thirty to fifty
yards from the ranch house The roof was of
heavy logs, deeply covered with earth, the
whole rising only foot above the level of the
ground.


Loopholes large enough to sight a rifle
through were cut on all sides. Thus the land
monitor presented these two essential ideas:
small and difficult target for the enemy, and
a circular protection from which to shoot
in all directions. An underground passage
from the ranch house led to the monitor
This passage was so low that one had to
crawl on hands and knees


Inside the monitor planks resting on
boxes gave the defenders support which
brought their heads and shoulders to the
level of the loopholes. Women and non
combatants sat on the floor in safety, When
the ranch house and the stable were in
flames or marauding Indians were battering
down the doors, the occupants took to the
monitor by underground passages. There
they found always a store of ammunition,
food, and water


These underground forts baffled the In
dams, who could not dig out or starve out
the garrisons. The besieged had perfect
range from which to fire on the besiegers,
and return fire was as futile as if directed
into sandpile. White puffs of smoke squirt
ing from the ground wore out the courage
and patience of the Indians. They did what
damage they could to property, but usually
drew off after short siege. Then the from
tiersmen came out from their holes, went to
building again, and in the end conquered the
West

All salads should be served very

ter and filled with shredded lettuce

Miss Grauel's recipe for cheese

rika; rub together with a tablespoon

Turn onto the Toured baking board and

oven and serve with the straws laid

Rich and elaborate salads are served

served on individual salad plates Very

About twenty citizens of southwest
Washington, through their attorney, w.
G. Johnson, filed an injunction suit yes
terday afternoon in the District Supreme
Court to compel the Philadelphia, Bal
timore and Washington Railroad Com
pany to tear down the bridge which had
been hastily constructed over Four-and-
a-half street, between D street and Vir-
ginia avenue southwest The bridge
connects the railroad yards with the coal
yards.


The indignant citizens have decided to
let the railroad complete the structure
and then have the courts order II torn
down. The bridge now is about COM
pleted. The steel glrders have been set
in place, and nothing remains to be done
but the masonry work.


Law Governs Erection.


The citizens complain that the erec-
ton Of the bridge will cause a decrease
in the value of surrounding property
and that the windows OF nearby stores
will have TO be kept shut to protect
goods from the flying coal dust and loco
motive smoke. They contend in their
petition to the court that the Com
missloners are unauthorized to approve
the erection of such a bridge.


Congress has provided by law" said
Attorney Johnson last night. where
and how railroads may erect such struc-
lures within the District Congress has
not provide for such a bridge, and the
Commissioners have no right to permit
the railroad to erect the structure"


Commissioner Judson said yesterday
that the law provides that coal yards
may be located along a line of railroad
tracks. He also said that there is al
ways protest from persons living in
neighborhoods where such yards are
erected. The Commissioner added that
the matter was given careful consIdera-
ton. however, and that 1t was finally
decided that the permit should be
granted.


The permit was granted March 81
Capt. Mark Brooke, Assistant Engineer
Commissioner. gave individual hearings
to the indignant citizens, but no formal
hearing was granted.

Preside. Tex. Jan. - VITA Maria, Jan.
20.-Fully one hundred OF the govern
ment's troops were killed in the fight two
days ago at Ojinaga. according to a mes
sage received here to-day.


A flying squadron Of rebels decoyed
large force under Colonel Dorantes. The
insurgents entered a narrow mountain
gorge. where the unsuspecting federal
troops followed.


When two hundred of the pursuing troops
had entered the gorge a deadly fire was
poured into them from the heights. Re
treat was ordered. but before Colonel Do
rantes's men could escape at least halt
their number had been killed and others
wounded


The government troops were caught in
trap and were moved down by the storm
OF bullets which swept their ranks from
three directions. The rebels occupied the
cliffs and mountains, and the soldiers were
in the road with only one way OF escape
and that blocked. or the two hundred
men who went into the pass only forty
escaped, as far as known. They joined the
column under Colonel Dorantes.


The insurgent loss is said TO have been
slight. only five men being killed, accord
ing 10 their reports.


The fighting started on January Is when
small band OF rebels was routed at Co
yama. column Of two hundred soldiers
pursued the fleeing insurgents and ran into
the trap set for them. The road winds
through a narrow canyon. into which the
government troops marched. When all
were in the pass the insurrectos swept
down the mountainside in the road behind
them and the firing began. II is believed
that about two hundred insurgents were
engaged. They lay behind rocks and
poured steady fire into the government
troops


A rebel detachment was seen after the
light with thirty-two captured Mauser
rifles


The battle lasted all day January Il. On
January IS Colonel Dorantes advanced
from Oinaga with reinforcements. He
circled about. avoiding the pass and en-
tered the mountains from the west. He
discovered the rebels and a continuous fight
for two days followed.


Dorantes then retired into the hills and
is now awaiting reinforcements.


Last night another column Of one hun
bred soldiers left Ojnaga for the relief OF
Dorantes Several wounded insurgents and
number OF injured soldiers have been
taken 10 San Juan. The insurrectos had
cared for the wounded soldiers. treating
them with the same consideration shown
their own men. There are about eight hun
bred soldiers and armed citizens Of the

YARMOUTH. Mass. August 49, 1911.


Representatives Of all the Puritan
families who originally settled the
Cape Cod peninsula are to be found in
every one Of the sixteen villages scat
tered along its coasts. Most of them
are in the churchyards, but the sur
vivors may be found In big. white
comfortable frame houses with green
blinds and neatly kept gardens around
them These houses were built sew
eral generations ago. but have been
kept up with such care that they are
rule. are much moro comfortable than
the "newfangled" cottages that have
been built between them during the
last few years.


The people who own and live In them
are the descendants Of the sea rovers
who made Cape Cod famous in every
foreign port and won for themselves
regulations for trading wisely and
well. Yankee shrewdness and thrift
were profitable to the present genera
tions as well as to those who have
passed And that explains the COM
Portable mansions that are no longer
needed for the families of the owners,
and therefore are given up to the sum-
mer boarders. who are now the chief
source of revenue of this section.


Great men have gone out from those
fine old mansions, not only sea kings
but empire builders. and the pioneers
OF our west-the men who have built
up New York. Chicago. Pittsburgh,
Cleveland. Cincinnati and the great
cities of the Pacific coast Yankee
shrewdness. enterprise and thrift GER
minated In the sand dunes Of Cape
Cod are no longer expended on the
seas, but you can see the result of
their application In the great trusts
that are giving so much concern to the
politician. in the great manufacturing
enterprises. in the railways, in the
banks and the mercantile establish
ments of every city of the central and
western states.

Halifax, N. s., July 25.-Badly buffeted by
severe storm that broke off the Nova
Scotia coast last night, the power boat
Caroline. owned by NJ. It. Dennis, and the
favorite In the reciprocity motorboat race
from New York to Halifax. crossed the
finish line off the Royal Nova Scotia 1acht

It had been expected that the winners
time would be about sixty hours, but the
Caroline was considerably under this esti-
mate. covering the 553 miles between
Gravcsend Bay and Halifax In exactly
nfty-seven hours


The Eronel was the second boat to finish
Sine arrived off the pier at $50 a. m, but
the weather was too thick for her skipper
70 make out the judges boat and she did
not cross the line officially until two hours
later, pulling UP her anchor and crossing
the line between the marks in order TO re
credited with an official finish.


The men on the Eronel reported having
experienced fine weather until last night
when the boat ran into a stiff southeaster,
accompanied by heavy seas, thunder and
lightning.


Snapshot III, the third contestant, had
not finished up to noon to-day, and, as
result of her non-appearance. the dance al
the yacht club in honor Of the racers
crews, which was to have been given to-

There was only few minutes difference
in the time allowances Of these three
boats The Tramp, which was the scratch
boat Of the four craft that started from
Gravesend Bay, withdrew from the race
somewhere in the vicinity Of Block Island.


The last part Of the CarOline's trip was
made under most unfavorable conditions.
Yesterday afternoon the wind blew in from
the southeast. increasing in intensity as
the night came on, and kicking UP tre-
mendous sea all along the Nova Scotia
coast. Part Of the time thick haze hung
over the sea, making observation difficult.
but the downpour Of rain which came later
cleared away the haze and made the lights
of the harbor beacon visible for miles.


As the Caroline rounded Cape Sambro,
several miles from here, the gale and sea
caused some trouble, breaking the wheel
ropes ard carrying away some canvas.
Entering the harbor, the Caroline, with
the wind astern, fairly flew up to the finish
line, but did not stop until oil the custom
house, we'll up the harbor. 1t was two
hours later before any one came ashore
from the craft.


Chief Officer Cane, OF the steamer Flon-
bel. who navigated the Caroline into port.
reported all hands well and most enthusi-
astic over their victory.


Mr.. Dennis, the owner OF the Caroline,
said to-day that he was willing TO race
back TO New York. His boat had a narrow
escape from being wrecked on the lodges
off Sambro last night. When the wheel
rope was broken during the gale. the Caro-
line swung perlously near the Lodges, but
the damage was repaired in time to set
the boat on her course again before any
accident happened.

double-headed freight train was passing

ern railway twenty miles west Of Lynch
burg this afternoon the front locomo-

colored section man from Bedford City,
received wounds from flying grate-bar
which caused his death tonight at hos
pital here.


William Rosser. a white fireman from
Roanoke, who was Scalded about the
face, head and back. was brought here
and his condition tonight is pronounced
critical. The cause of the explosion is
not known. Severed other persons re-
ceived minor injuries. but did not re-
quire hospital attention.

Laura z. Sheck. twenty years old
today filed suit for limited divorce from
her husband, Raymond E. Sheck. She
charges cruelty and desertion, and asks
alimony and counsel fees.


Mrs. Sheck says she was married June
q. 1909. and that her husband deserted
her in Baltimore August following.
Being without means of support. the wife
says she went to the home of her hus-
bands parents. where she lived until
August last. Then, she states. she re-
turned to her parents, who have since
supported her.


The wife says during the short time her
husband lived with her he came home in
an intoxicated condition. illtreated and
abused her. and caused her bodily and
mental suffering and humiliation.


Attorney d. Edward Clarke appears for
the wife.

MALTA, October "A scene of conSid-
cradle confusion occurred at the quaran-
tine station here shortly after midnight
this morning. when the British steamer
Castlegarth entered the harbor i'm the
height of a severe gale. crowded with
1,3G0 Maltese refugees from Tripoli. The
1900 passengers were huddled on the
deck clamoring to get to land after three
days with an insufficient supply of food
and water Although there had been no
casualties. practically all of the refugees
were faint from hunger and thirst.


The port authorities promptly ordered
emergency measures, directing the vessel
to dock immediate ly. Once ashore, the
passengers found. relief soon forthcom-
ing. i -.


The members of the Maltese colony in
Trfpoli went aboard the Castlegarth Fri
DAY morning at the suggestion of the
British consul, who feared for their
safety in the threatened commandment.
Their provisions we're soon exhausted and
the severe weather added to their discom-
fort. The storm continued with severity
throughout their three days on the water.


Although the passengers boarded the
Castlegarth Friday morning, the vessel
did not leave Tripoli until IL o'clock Sat
urday night. Up to that time the Ital-
ians had not bombarded the city or land
ed troops. The Italian admiral, however
had warned the captain of the Castle
garth Saturday afternoon that he would
not guarantee the safety of the ship after
sunset. The Italian consul and other Off
Gals boarded the Italian flagship. The
consuls of the other powers went on
board an English vessel. Telegraph OPP

after the firing was concluded the Off

men or more were killed in a desperate
battle between the Mexican federal SOL
diers and a small party Of insurrectos
on the bank Of the Rio Grande opposite
this point yesterday. The insurrectos had
only eighteen men, and for three hours
they held at bay about seventy-five
.rurales and about 100 infantry soldiers.
When darkness ended the battle the in
surrectos held the field. and the federal
troops had withdrawn a couple of miles
and camped. The insurrectos left a
couple of hours later for their mountain
headquarters. fifty miles away, carrying
their wounded with them. They had
buried their dead.


OF the eighteen insurrectos. two were
killed and seven wounded. f. s. O'Reil-
~. correspondent with the insurrectos,
received slight wound In the thigh.


Twice the rurales charged the insurgent
position. once coming within fifty yards.
but each time they were REFUSED. the
correspondent counted eighteen federal
soldiers that were carried from the field
during the battle.


Reinforcements Save Little Band.


The arrival Of twenty more insurrectos
In the last few minutes Of the fight saved
the defenders and prevented what prob
ably would have been a massacre OF the
little band.


The report from government sources
that detachment of insurrectos had
crossed the river and fired on the soldiers
from the American side is denied by the
insurrectos So far as is known, only one
man crossed the river to the American
side. the press correspondent. and he did
not do SO until two hours after the bat
tie. under cover of darkness.


The insurrectos have a strongly forti-
ned camp in the mountains, with more
than $50 men under arms at that point.
They are well armed and plentifully sup
piled with ammunition.


Stop Movement Of Trains.

main body Of the insurrectos, under Pas
cual Orozco, is about fourteen miles. west

sas City. Mexico and Orient railroad
line. There are 200 federal troops here,
but the main body, under Gen. Navarro,
Numbering over LOCO. is at Guerrero. nine
miles distant Navarro apparently is

trains until further notice. Mining men.

Word was received at the war depart
ment today that Gen. Luque had occu-

opposition from the insurrectos The
force under Gen. Navarro Is said to be

TON. L. l.. April s.-The life savers
private telephone line stretching along
the sandy beach of Long Island this
evening brought here the story of a
exciting fight with it. The Southamp-
ton life savers reported that early this
morning they sighted a leviathan a
few miles off shore and put out in a
small boat in pursuit. The whale,
however, was too speedy, and they lost
it.

Word Of the chase had been sent to
Amagansett, where the whale was
sighted shortly after noon. A start was
made in pursuit. and Capt. Edwards
finally shot the harpoon into the whale
amidship.


The whale dived, raced, came up and
soon was pulling the Amagansett crew
at lightning pace through the sea. AZ
ter all the line had gone the crew
commenced to pull in, intending to
get alongside the whale and deal the
death blow.


Whale Smashes the Boat.


But as the boat pulled up near the
whale the latter gave a terrific lash
ing and it's tail smashed into the boat.
The harpoon line was cut and while
the whale made for deep sea the boat
turned for the shore. In the surf the
boat broke in two and the men had
to swim for shore, which they made
after hard struggle.

A Boston woman has gone to Africa
to hunt lions.


As though there were not plenty OF
big game right here at home!


Women all around US are hunting
lions every day.


There Is the woman whose life n
being fried away with the evening POI
tatoes. She knows that when Sunday
comes, the best that can come from
the differences between the high cost
of living" and weekly wage is car
ride to the park. And each day she


bags the lion Of envy, the lion Of
jealousy, the lion OF unrest-just for
the sake OF those about her whom she


loves and who love her and for whom
she is willing to sacrifice and to toll.
There is the girl in the store who
handles rich silks all day and who goes
home at night to wash her cotton shirt
waist that 1t may be fresh on the NOR
row. She has her lions to slay. She
knows that other girls are slipping
cooling drinks In some restaurant,
listening to seductive music, smiled
upon and petted. But she knows the
night the thought that the Easier
Way is the better one and she saves
her own conscience and her own self
respect from the beast Of temptation.
In fact every woman who 10 doing
useful work in the world Is also
Zion hunting" She hunts them In her
own life.


She kills the thoughts that are more
ravenous than any beast.
She kills the temptations that would
destroy her ideals.


Jungle women? Why, they save the


world over and over again every day.

equally as important is its work OF

joints the uratic impurity with which

duces the aches and stiffness which
always accompany the disease. Like
wise the muscles are coated and lose
their elasticity, while the continual
irritation to the nerves produces
swelling and Inflammation of the flesh.

Frederick, Md, Aug. I8-What this

left Washington before the troops en-

PITTSBURG, January N.-It became
known today that while the family Of
William Thaw, jr.. were at dinner last
night the residence was robbed of jewels
to the value of $4,000. Included among
the valuables is a pearl necklace worth
$1,000. the property Of Mrs. Thaw.


Mrs Thaw had been to the closet where
her Jewels were kept half an hour before
dinner, with a view to selecting those she
would wear last night. Only her maid
was in the room, and, after locking the
door as usual, Mrs. Thaw Joined the
family in the dining room. She was alb
sent perhaps thirty minutes, and upon
her return went to the closet for the
pearl necklace. The door was locked.
but when she looked for the necklace 1t
was gone Hastily opening the other
cases. she discovered all had been emptied
of their contents.


Screaming that her jewels were gone
Mrs. Thaw aroused the household. and 1t
was seen that the thieves had taken
nothing but the contents of the closet. A
hurried call was sent to the police. and
personal supervision of the superintend-
ent. are working on the case, while a
score or more plain clothes men are
securing the city in search Of suspects.


Servants Are Questioned.


When the detectives reached the house
each servant was separately and carefully
examined. but no information concerning
the robbery was given. There was no
evidence that the house had been entered,
yet the time OF each person In 1t was sat
isfactorily accounted for.


Recently the number OF servants in the
Thaw household has been gradually re-
duced. there being only two housekeep-
ers and two maids employed at this time.
The police believe that some one, well ac-
quainted with the interior OF the house,
had entered by skeleton key, and with
another key of the same character had
unlocked the door of the jewel closet and
stolen all 1t contained.


Mrs Thaw is a sister-in-iaw OF Harry
Kendall Thaw. who was tried for shoot
ing Stanford White, the New York archi-
tect.

bed by two highwaymen about midnight

bers entered the mail car, held up the
clerks and looted the car. They stopped

escape.


Posses were searching for them west

highwaymen pulled the emergency sig

then leaped from the mail car and dis
appeared down the village street


The conductor Is positive that the out
laws boarded the train here, but whether
they crawled on the roof Of or swung onto
the platform he does not know.


The first intimation the mail clerks had
of the attack was when the door of the
car swung suddenly open, ana they 1ouno
themselves faced by the highwaymen. No
one attempted resistance as the intrud-
ers proceeded to the looting of the sacks.


The conductor and engineer OF the train
had no inkling OF any trouble until the
signal to stop at Yoncalla was sounded,
and the mail clerks raised the alarm.


officers here and the sheriff at Koseburg

Sir: When February comes and an un-

frost lacks it's bitter sting; when even
country life seems unnatural and more soli-
tary than ever; as some clear and moon
less night reisns TRANQUILITY over vale and
hill. we leave our comfortable freside ana
wander beneath the sparkling. sleepless
stars.


We gaze into the zenith. admiring not
far away Queen Capellss pure brillancy
and the united stars Of Pleiades we
glance az ruddy Aldebaran. and then thrill
with enthusiasm over spectacular Orion and
scintillating Sirius We look eastwardly.
kenning solitary Procyon and inseparable
Castor and Pollux We seek Rezulus ana
think OF Arcturus. sweep over the Dipper.
Draco and Ursa Minor. and turning west
wardly. cross Cepheus. Cassiopeia. the
Milky Way. part Of Andromeda and Aries.
till, reaching Perseus, we fnd ourselves
back at Capella and Pleiades We have
surveyed our armament of night. viewed a
scintillating and spectacular sidereal spec
tacle. and return 10 our comfortable fire.
side. well repaid for this nocturnal ramnle

NEW YORK, May 1o.-The steamship
Merida Of the Ward line, with POI pas
sengers. from Havana for this city. was
rammed by the steamer Admiral Farra-
gut from Philadelphia for Port Antonio
The Merida's passengers and crew were
transferred to the Admiral Farragut.


Water poured through the gaping
wound in the Meridas side, and five
hours after the collision the steamship
settled beneath the waves. Wireless dis
tress signals were flashed in every di-
rection and the United States battleship
Iowa hurried to the Merida's assistance.

ilton later came alongside the Admiral
Farragut, according to a wireless dis

morning. and took the Marida's S passen-
gers and crew Off the Farragut. The
Hamilton will arrive at Norfolk late to-
day.


Floating on Fore Bulkheads.

Nader of the Admiral Farragut stated:


'Farragut floating on fore collision bulk
heads. United States ships Iowa and
Hamilton coming to our assistance


This wireless message led to the belief
that the Farragut had been damaged,
possibly seriously. in the collision.


The following message from Capt. Rob-
ertson of the Merida came to the United
Wireless Company here:


Merida and Admiral Farragut in col
lfsion at 12:3U o'clock this morning. All

dering public service.

landing.

miral Barry received an Associated Press
reporter, to whom he denied in general and
emphatic terms the stories which have
been published concerning the reasons for
his unexpected retirement from the navy.

York, where he expects to make his
home.

feet, with the California as his flagship,

along in a great elliptic path around the
sun. When the earth in its motion of
more than eighteen miles second col

burned up by its friction with our air,
and appears as bright, swiftly moving
Star-like object.

variable stars, ever changing. growing
brighter and then fainter, are two of
the most interesting celestial phenome-
ma of this summers season. and we'll

LIVERPOOL. Aug. I6.A mob tonight
attacked and damag ged the motor wagons
carrying newspaper supplies in Scotland
road. The infantry fixed bayonets and
formed a square about the motors until
damages were repaired while the police
dispersed the mob with their clubs There
were many arrests.


The strike committee called out the
men on the stree, railway and mobs
smashed the window panes Of cars tha I
were left standing in the streets.


The outbreaks throughout the day.
however. we're few and not very serious
the fatal shooting by the troopers yester-
day had n good moral effect and the mere
approach Of soldiers to-day was enough
to send the hoodlums scurrying through
the side streets. There are now $500
soldiers here.


There remains a general tension. and
1t is only the presence of the troops that
keeps down the mobs


The menace from famine has not
abated Many small traders have sold out
completely and are unable to get more
supplies. Several -four mills have stopped
because they cannot get coal and bread
is most dufficult to get in some places
The big hotels and restaurants are feeling
the pinch. while IN the poorest parts Of
the city the people are actually threat
ened with starvation.


The authorities are interested chiefly in
the situation in the district within the
radius Of mile of Scotland road. where
the poorest people live and where the
perpetual enmity that exists between
Roman Catholics and Orangemen has
been responsible in the past for many
desperate fights. These quondam rivals
have now joined hands against a common
enemy. the police and soldiers The
temper OF the population of this district
led the military commanders to order
the soldiers, il called upon to fire. not to

but to let every bullet find its mark.


Two Of the City Corporations milk

In their half of the seventh, the Christians
failed to score. Wasn't it fourteen to six,
and out of their six the Jews had not earned
run? The Jews faced the Christians He
brew pitcher for their half of the seventh.
The first two to the bat made scratchy hits,
the third got base on balls, the fourth
made a two-bagger, and what with errors
and overthrows from the Christian sleepers
in the field, four runs were scored and it
stood fourteen to ten. Things repeated
themselves, and the bases were again filled.
But then the Hebrew ally of the Christians
struck out the next two men in six pitched
balls. The tenth Jew to go to the bat was
little red headed Hester-st. lad.


This diminutive specimen was what a
bystander called the Yom Kippur Short
stop; but, in spite of his short arms and
legs, the little chap felded his position in
fine shape. Carrots, his friends called at
The din was something appalling. Now,
Carrots had been numerous times at the
bat and so far had merely famed the air,
not even connecting for foul tip with the
ball. AS he stepped to the plate some one
handed him another bat, this one so large
that as he rested it on the ground the handle
swept his nose. The racket was earsplitting.
The pitcher swung in one ball, and Carrots
never even saw it pass him. Then the
pitcher took pity on the little chap and
tossed him an easy one. But Carrots
swung his bat viciously this time and, re-
markable, uncanny even, he connected with
the sphere and out it sailed into space
toward Mosholu Parkway two miles off.


The three Christian outhelders raced after
the ball. The boomerang from the hit laid
little Carrots out fiat; so much so that he
did not know what he had done. But those
Jew rooters were there, and they yelled at
him to run. Carrots picked himself up and
off his little legs went, the mob following in
a bunch, yelling like demons. The three
other Jews were home by the time Carrots
had reached second. But the ball could not
be found and Carrots tottered across the
home plate, mouth open, hair flying, and
fell into the arms of his adoring Hester-st
comrades, the hero of the day. The next
Jew struck out, and the score was tie,
inning made off those sleepy Christians!


The eighth inning found the Gentiles so
demoralized and the Hebrews playing such
snappy ball that the former went out in
one-two-t three order. The first two Jews in
their half went out on strikes, and the third,
their best hitter, popped an easy fly which
the Christian second baSeman allowed to
60 through his hands as if they were made of
butter, then overthrow to first, and what
with other errors and fumbles the Jew came
home, scoring what proved to be the win
ming run. The next Jew up struck out.


A storm that had been gathering all after
noon broke furiously and everyone ran to
cover. The umpire, Christian, waited the
prescribed time under the rules, when
the field was like lake, and called the game
at the end of the eighth inning in favor of
the Hester-st. players, fifteen to fourteen.

Milestones that have been in the ground

the old Philadelphia and Pittsburg pike
are being unearthed in most unexpected
places Recently the farmers of Cum
berland county have taken up the matter
and are trying to aid those who are MAX
ing the investigation.


At meeting near Hogestown members
of the organization stated that all but two
of the stones between Harrisburg and
HosestOwn had been located. One of the
stones, it was discovered, had been used
for some years as weight for a har-
row. The search for the other two stones
will he made. Those that have been found
will be reset soon. The stones were
originally placed between 1910 and 1916

Florence Carey, the sixteen-year- old girl
who in the past month has escaped three
times from the House of the Good Shep-

her. was yesterday placed on conditional
probation by Judge De Lacy of the Juvenile
Court with the understanding that she
become her fathers housekeeper. and

Carey, a stationary engineer. has the new
home equipped. Florence will remain in
the home Of Mrs. Florence Rollins SIT

her in the past.

charged from the Emergency Hospital,
where she had been patient for ten days,
suffering from sprained ankle and nu-
merous bruises. the result Of jumping from
a third-story window at. the home the
last time she escaped. Immediately

established home, with Florence at the
head of it, the court ordered the girls

text:
NEW LONDON. Conn, July liar
wards effort to sweep the Thames yes
terday for the third consecutive year was
not quite accomplished, for although the
Crimson won the great varsity events in
runaway style by nineteen lengths, and
the substitute VARSITY four b. five
lengths. the Yale freshmen captured the
initial event.


In each race the winning crew led from
the start and Harvard's giant varsity
eight shook off the lighter Yale crew at
the start. and was never again challenged
throughout the four miles


1t was the fourth consecutive victory
of the big crew for Harvard. a record
that has not come TO Cambridge for
nearly half century.


The varsity race was rowed down
stream with a favorable tide. but with
head breeze that made progress somewhat
slow.


The morning races were rowed up
stream. also with the tide but against a
moderate wind, and those times were slow
as well.


Times Of the Races.


The official times for the three races
were:


Varsity race-Harvard, 2om. AS; Yale,
23m. 4Olas.


Freshmen-Yale, lin. 53s.; Harvard.
lin. 591ks.


Varsity fours-Harvard 13m 376s. !;
Yale, 18Th. 52s.


The varsity race was witnessed by more
than $500 people on shore. in observa-
ton trains. and on the river in a gayly
decorated floating grandstand. Overhead
lowered an aeroplane. while beneath stole
submarine, which escaped the vigilance
Of the marine policemen.


Referee Meikleham waited half an hour
after the scheduled time for the wind to
subside and then sent the varsity Fights
away from the moOred punts opposite
Red Top at $50 o'clock.


Harvard caught the water first. and the
initial stroke showed the power Of its
crew. A yard was gained there, and this
lead was increased to more than a length
before the half mile was reached.


Yale Lacked the Power.


Yale rowed in perfect form and rhythm.
but power was lacking. Every Harvard
stroke meant a gain. and this continued
down to the very finish The crews met
rough water between the mile and two
mile flags, and both dropped the stroke
to an even thirty.


After leaving the navy yard. however.
the Yale stroke was hit up to thirty-three
and even thirty-five for a few minutes
but there was no perceptible gain, and
Harvard was then far ahead.


Shouts were few and far between owing
to the runaway nature Of the race until
the Harvard crew was almost at the line.
Then cannon doomed, whistles screeched.
the crowds cheered and the Harvard
oarsmen padded over the line as If they
had been canoeing. while Coxswain
Ables swung around in his seat for
first and distant view of the Yale shell.
Yale athletic experts shook their heads
gloomily and said that Yale was surpris-
ingly inferior.


Yale Game to the End.


Yale rowed the race out, although the
oars trailed in limp fingers. The only
consolation that Yale obtained through
out the day was in the freshman race.
There the crews were so close for mile
and a half Of the two miles that only
those on the referees boat could pick
the leader


Persons on the observation trains, be-
cause of the poor range, gave Harvard
the lead for three-quarters of the race.
At the half mile, mile and mile and
half Yale's advantage in each case was
one second. In the homestretch the blue
youngsters pulled away and won by two
lengths The Harvard four evened the
score by jumping away from the Yale
shell at the start and holding con-
stantly increasing lead finishing with
four lengths between the shells.

NEW YORK, February 1s.--In a col
lision in the Narrows today between the
steamer Bayamo. just In from Santa Cruz.
and the steel barge Caddo both vessels
were damaged above the wate line. No
one was injured.


The Bayamo was getting under way
after her release from quarantine and
was making full speed astern across the
channel, when the tug Atkins, outward
bound with the Caddo in tow, attempted
to go under the liners stern. The Bay
amos sternway, deep laden and heavy as
she was, was too great for the quickly
reversed engines to check in time, and
the steamer struck the barge on the star
board bow, rolling her over to port until
her rail was nearly submerged.


The barge, being light. was pushed
away with slight damage, but the Bayamo
had her steering gear carried away and
the overhang of her stern crushed in.
Immediately after the collision she
dropped anchor off Stapleton.

The death of Justice Harlan will give

Court during his term Of office. Since he
assumed the presidency, in 1909, he has
already named four associate justices,

justice to the chief justiceship. The sue
cessor to Justice Harlan will be the fifth

the highest court.


Only once before has this occurred.
President Lincoln between 1862 and 1864
named five members Of the Supreme
Court. including one chief justice. These
were Associate Justices Swayne. Miller,
Davis and Field and Chief Justice Chase.
President Grant in 1904 named four
members of the court, Associate Justices
Strong, Bradley and Hunt and Chief
Justice Waite. President Harrison in
1SS9-93 named four associate justices,
Brewer, Brown. Shiras and Jackson.


OF the eight surviving members of the
court today the appointments came from
the following-named Presidents: Chief
Justice White, from President Cleveland
as associate and President Taft as chief
Associate Justices McKennas and Day
from President Mckinley; Associate JUS
tice Holmes. from President Roosevelt
Associate Justices Lurton. Hughes, Van
Devanter and Lamar, from Presiden
Taft

the last Of the elder jurists from the


bench. The member Of longest service is
| Chief Justice White. who was serving in
his eighteenth year in the court He il

LOUISBURG, c. B., March 2-Three
persons perished in the wreck of the
Newfoundland mail steamer Bruce,
which struck the rocks off Scatteri during
the night.


The Bruce was on her way from Port
aux Basques to this place at the time
Of tie disaster.


The Bruce ordinarily plies between Port
but owing to the ice fields In Cabot
strait the steamer for several weeks has
been using Louisburg as her Nova Sco-
tia terminus.


The Bruce, which left Port aux Bas-
ques late Wednesday night carrying 125
passengers, was delayed by drift ice and
rough seas. This forenoon word came
from Scatteri Island, twenty miles east
of LOuisburg. that the Bruce had struck
the rocks Off the coast Of the island last
night and that three lives had been lost.
The steamers bottom is badly damaged,
but there was hope of saving the vessel
The steamer struck heavily in the dark
ness Of the night at Port Nova Point. \
high gale prevailed, and great seas swept
the decks constantly.


In the attempt to save the passengers
the steamers crew worked heroically un-
der severe conditions, the extreme cold
boat was washed away, but finally all
hands except three men who were swept
away were landed. The women and chill
dren were taken ashore first.


This morning the Bruce was clear of
the rocks and was af1oat, but her ulti-
mate fate was somewhat in doubt, as
there were several feet Of water in one
of her compartments.


The Bruce was built at Glasgow, Scot
land, in 1897, for Sir Robert Reid of St
Johns. n. F., the principal owner of the
railway and steamship lines Of the Reid
Newfoundland Company. She is 1855
feet long, 32.6 feet beam aand 124 feet
deep.


She Is a steel ship with single screw
She was built on the lines of a yacht and
Is equipped with wireless apparatus.

Maria Pia, the Dowager Queen OF
Portugal who died recently At the
home Of her sister. Princess Clothilde,
at Moncalissi. near Turin. was a far
greater parsonage, and, historically, far
more important than contemporaneous
far more So than her easy-going, pleas
ure-lovins husband. King Luiz Be-
sides. she had indomitable courage, and
was brave and fearless. bordering on
recklessness. On one occasion, when she
was boating at the mouth of the Tagus
River with her two sons, they both fell
into the water while leaning over the
side. The gentlemen of her party did
not know how to swim-neither did the
Queen, for that matter-but she instantly
Jumped in after her two boys


She held on to the boat with one hand,
caught Prince Carlos Che crown prince)
with the other and contrived to lay hold
of the frock of little Prince Alfonso with
her teeth. AS she threw herself over
board she recollected how once she had
seen Newfoundland dog belonging to her
brothers, Prince Humbert, later King of
Italy, and the Duke OF Agosta, seize
with its teeth a drowning boy in Lake
Annecy. Her prompt courage and pres
ence Of mind certainly earned the gold
medal that the Lisbon Humane Society
awarded her. though. Of course. the rare
heroism she displayed had for its OBJ
ject her two sons. They were all the
dearer to her. for the loss of four chill
dren, one after another. in a way so un-
accountable that Miquelist tthe pretend
er partys) poisoners were suspected.


Maria Pia showed pluck and decision
on a great occasion while she was
though bride-yet in her teens. One
morning at daybreak Marshal saldanha,
who had won his rank mostly IN pronun-
ciamentos and street fights. forced hts
way into the royal sleeping apartments
and there dictated a decree comforting
upon his military omnipotence. together
with a considerable increase in salary
He had cxtorted before such increases
from the King by threats to dethrone
him. The Queen at once adjured the
King to order the execution of Saldanha
The officer he had left in the ante
chamber witnessed the scene through the
open door. They owned afterward that
the Queens energy had affected them
so powerfully that had she taken upon
herself to issue the order they would
have led the marshal into the courtyard
and shot him. But the King signed the
decree-worse luck to him.


Maria Pia, on that sinister morning,
must have been the beau ideal of a
tragedy queen. She then had a fine, tall
figure. The masses OF Titian-red hair
frizzled naturally and seemed visibly af-
fected by every strong emotion. Her
eyes had an intensity of expression, and
their brillancy enhanced their keen pene-
tration. She loved display. Partisan ele-
gance. and minute order in all but her
finances. She never minced her words in
but had a compassionate
and generous heart.


She domineered over her court and
family, and stood on her rights with her
son, King Carlos, and her daughter-in-
law when they wanted her TO give up TO
them the AJuda palace. which her mar
riage contract had secured for her for
life. Dom Manuel, the present eXiled
King OF Portugal, from his infancy was
the object OF her idolatrous love. Her

From the Columbian.


China is not the only example of a
nation or state which has paid dearly for
neglecting the military art. In all ages
of the world history has taught the same
lesson. The people hardened TO war have
triumphed over those who devoted them
selves wholly to peaceful pursuits. The
military machine has rolled like jugger-
naut over communities whose chief con-
Germ was with commerce. luxury and
learning Sparta vanquished Athens, and
degenerate HellaS was absorbed by Rome
Rome itself fell when the Romans ceased
to be their own defenders. Modern his
tory has witnessed no change in the rela-
tive position of militant and nOn-militant
nations. The great powers Of Europe are
keyed up to their highest point Of war
like efficiency because they know and feel
that they cannot otherwise maintain their
prestige and command respect for their
rights. The German kaiser and the late
King Edward have been Listened to with
respect and approval when they declared
themselves champions of universal peace
because the former had behind him the
most formidable army and the latter the
most formidable navy in the world. With
out that army and that navy their words
would have made but little impression.


War is g. terrible evil, but from it's en-
sanguined fields springs forth the flower
Of liberty, and the nation that would be
free must ever be prepared for the sac
rifices that war entails. The millennium
of universal peace will not come at the
touch OF Mr.. Carnegie's golden wand
That it will come eventually all right
Meantime it Is both right and duty to
follow the injunction of the hard-headed
Puritan warrior to Put your trust in
God and keep your powder dry"

Special Correspondence OF The Star.


DUBLIN, September 8, 1911.


A strike Of newsboys began here several
days ago. 1t was director against the
Evening Herald. Before o'clock on a Fri
day, when the second edition of that Jour-
nal comes out, the boys. to the number of
several hundred. large percentage of
them with bare feet, assembled opposite
the Independent and Herald Offices in Mid
die Abbey street, and awaited the vana
laden with the papers. There we're few
police about at the time, most of them be-
ing at the railway stations and the North
Wall in connection with the railway
strike. When the vans appeared the boys
proceeded to attack them, held up the
horses and threw the parcels into the
street. where they were furiously torn to
pieces and scattered to the wind.


The following day the situation was
much worse. The lads again gathered
outside the Herald Office, and no edition
came out. The attack was next directed
against the Mail. which was completely
driven off the streets.

man predicted it would be even hotter

terday by the fact that 1t was a day
of rest, with all free to seek the most
sheltered spots in which to escape the
suns ravages. Today. with early con-
ditions threatening a new heat rec
ord, the health authorities declared
their fear that another record also
would be set-a new high mark of
deaths and prostrations from the
weather for the greater city.

Every shore resort within reach of
the city was thronged with swelterins
humanity all last night, while the city
parks, hOusetops, and tenement fire
escapes were crowded as never before.

people rolled and tossed through the
terrible hours, while special details OF
police patrolled their sleeping lines to
keep off the prowling thieves that al
ways seize advantage of such opportu-
mites.

thermometer, far above the intense
pavement heat waves, a maximum
temperature of 4.5 degrees was reached
at 4:30 yesterday afternoon. On the
sidewalks the mercury at that time was
at the 107 mark. Worse than this, how
ever, was the terrible humidity, more
than 30 degrees above the normal.

Special Dispatch to The Star


BRANDYWINE, Prince Georges county,
Md, May 13.-Residents of this section
of the county have experienced exciting
times with forest fires since Wednesday
night Several times the fires have been
extinguished, and this morning they broke
out again in several places. necessitating
quick action to prevent serious damage.
Thursday night and last night the
Pennsylvania Railroad Company officials
sent gangs of trackmen here to fight the
flames. The fire burned on both sides of
the tracks of the Popes Creek branch OF
the company, but the fire-fghters. track
men and volunteers, were able to prevent
the burning of the ties.


Peril to Railroad Service.


The railroad schedule was not inter-
fer ed with by reason of the several
fires, but the condition Of affairs this
afternoon makes it appear that the rail-
road may be put out of commission be-
fore tomorrow.


Dense clouds of black smoke are curl
ing from the wooded land below this
town, and the town is also filled with
smoke. The blaze this afternoon has
reached q point within one-half mile of
the town, and railroad men and county
residents are doing their best to get it
unuer control before night.


Hundreds OF pine trees that We're blown
down during the blizzard two years ago
furnished material for the flames The
trees are dry and they assist in sending
along the flames at a furious rate, The
fire has already covered an area Of more
than 500 acres, much cord wood and
many railroad ties having been destroyed.
Thus far the fire has not reached any
buildings, although several of them mar
rowly escaped being burned.

Austin. Penn. Sept. 30.-Between 800
and 1000 persons were drowned and
untold numbers were manned here this
afternoon when the great dam of the
Bayless Pulp and Paper Company, hold
ing back more than five hundred million
gallons of water. went out.


Forty bodies have been recovered.
many of them so MANNED that recog-
nitlon is impossible.


Governor John X. Tener Of Pennsyl-
vania has been asked for help, and re-
lief train was sent from Coudersport'
four miles away.


The survivors are in a frenzy. There
ia no organization, the town being dazed
by the force Of the calamity, which came
without a moments warning.


Hundreds of men, women and children
are searching through the ruins of the
village for their families and friends.


Broken Gas Pipes Set Fire.


The only light is the glare from hun
dreds Of houses and business buildings,
which caught fire from broken gas pipes
almost before the flood had passed.


Chaos reigned from the moment the
mighty wall of water tore through the
town, and there will be no relief until
help comes from the surrounding towns.
Meantime many bodies lie in the track
Cf the flood.


The dam was built two years ago. 1t
was a great structure. $50 feet long,
spanning the little valley formed by
Freeman Run; and rising 10 the height
of forty-nine feet. 1t was of concrete,
thirty-two feet wide at the base, and
said to be constructed after the most APP
proved plans Of modern engineering.
TIL, basin behind it had never been filled
with water until this week, and to-day
it was noticed that water was running
over the top of the structure. Many
persons went out from the town, mile
and half away, to see the unusual
sight. and il was while they were watch
ing the overhowing water that the first
break occurred.

The little town Of Costello, below this
place. has been annihilated. The popu-
lation is between 400 and 800 persons.
survivor who reached Austin at 10
o'clock tonight said that there was
hardly sign OF life in Costello.
Whether most Of the citizens perished
in the flood or fed to the hills the man
could not say. He believes, however,
that two-thirds Of the population are
dead. Practically every building in the
town was levelled by the torrent which
came from Austin.


Definite Information was obtained
after 10 o'clock that every member Of
the family Of State Senator Frank f.
Baldwin. except the Senator himself,
was killed. These include Mrs. Baldwin,
their children, Senator Baldwin's
mother, father and sister. The Senator
was injured.


The flames are sweeping the entire
town at 10 o'clock, and only the hospital
and schoolhouse, on a hill, will escape
destruction.

New York. Nov. 3o-Before a cheering
crowd of more than 5000 persons, Sidney
Hatch, of Chicago, won the fifth annual
Yonkers Marathon race this afternoon,
covering the distance in two hours thirty
five minutes and twenty seconds. Hatch
was representing the Illinois State Gaelic
Athletic Association, Of Chicago.


William Calvin, Of the Mercury A. c.,
of Yonkers, was second; ]. j. Reynolds,
of the Irish-American A. c., of New York,
third, and James Cleary, of the Ottawa
A. c., of Worcester, Mass, fourth.


The final struggle for the victory was a
hard one, and the distance between the
first four men but slight. About sixteen
miles Of the race was run through the
streets of Yonkers at such a clip that
thirty of the fifty-seven contestants had
dropped out before the leaders turned
into the old Empire race track for the
final laps.


Cleary led the contestants in the race
and increased his speed, but the others in
the first bunch pulled up and soon passed
the Massachusetts man. Calvin and
Hatch fought bitterly for the lead for two
laps. Hatch finally took first place with
the Yonkers man still running gamely.
Conditions for the race were ideal.

Not only is the blood the great
nourishing source of our systems. but
equally as important is its work of
removing the waste of oxidMed It's
sues which have been consumed in
force and bodily heat. This waste is
filtered out through the kidneys.
When. however. the kidneys become
weak and unable to perform their
regular duties, the waste is allowed
to remain in the circulation, soon
forming uric acid. which destroys the
greater portion of nourishing ele-
ments of the blood and leaves it weak
and acrid. This imperfect blood de-
posts into the different muscles and
Joints the uratic impurity with which
it is contaminated. Then the pains
and aches of Rheumatism commence.
The gritty formation which uric acid
causes collects in the joints, pro-
duces the aches and stiffness which
always accompany the disease. Like
wise the muscles are coated and lose
their elasticity. while the continual
irritation to the nerves produces
swelling and inflammation of the flesh.

Washington, despite the heat which
has enveloped. the entire United States,
has Jared better than most cities The
number of fatalities and prostrations
have been small and upon several days
more than dozen cities throughout
the country experienced degree of
| torridity far beyond the record here
We have never yet been compelled 70
say that Washington was the hottest
place in the United States This un-
enviable distinction has twice been ac-
corded to Baltimore, for instance, once
last week, when the fact was reported
in the Baltimore Sun, and again on
July 3, when the Baltimore News dis
played in large headlines the announce
ment that Baltimore and New York led
all the rest in the matter of high tenn
perature.


The escape of the National Capital
from the excessive heat which has been
prevalent elsewhere is easily explained
In the first place, the wide streets offer
opportunity for a free circulation of
air, while nearly 100000 trees along
all the thoroughfares afford maximum
of delightful shade In addition to this,
Rock Creek Park and the Geological
Park, containing over 1000 acres, and
Immediately contiguous to the city, cover
vast expanse of country over which
the intensity of the heat is materially
reduced. The same may be said of the
parks throughout the city, and espe-
cially the Mall, extending from the
Capitol to the Washington Monument,
and supplemented by Potomac Park,
large open area of many hundred acres
along the river front. These are more
than mere breathing places. They are
effective in keeping down the tenn
perature, and the wisdom of their ac-i
QUESTION was never better demonstrated
than during the hot wave


The fact that there have been so few
deaths and prostrations is the best evi-
dence that Washington, even in summer
and under trying conditions, is to be
envied among cities.

OGDEN, Utah, Jan. 3-Posses carried
by special train and automobiles are
hunting today for two bandits who held
up Overland Limited train, No /, on the
Southern Pacific, at 11:50 o'clock last
night, nine miles from this city, shot
the porters, killing one, and looted the
Passengers of a large amount of money
and jewelry estimated at $4,000.


The bandits, who were masked and
heavily armed, signaled the train near
Reese Station with a lighted fuse. One
man climbed into the cab and pushed a
revolver into the face of the engineer.
Both the engineer and firemen were
ordered from the cab and obeyed.


The trainmen were ordered to the rear
of the train while the bandits entered
the sleeping cars. AS they were clam
bering on the vesubule steps two por-
ters appeared.


You men keep off this train." cried
one of the porters.


Bullets Answer Porters.


The men paid no attention to this
command but climbed to the platform.
The porters, who could not see dis
tinctly in the darkness, tried to push the
men down the steps. The robbers fired
several shots and both porters fell.
One was killed and the other seriously
wounded.


The passengers, aroused from their
sleep by the shots, crowded forward.
The bandits ordered them back.


Women screamed and became hys-
terical, and men were cowed by the
menacing guns in the hands of the men.
One bandit, with a huge revolver in
each hand, stood at the end of car
while the other went through, the pas
Bengers dumping jewelry and money
into a gunny sack.


Shortly after midnight Conductor Gun,
ningham made his escape and ran al
the way to the nearest station, where
word was flashed to Ogden, that the
Overland, the most celebrated train or
the Southern Pacific had been held up.


The bandits, after collecting theil
booty, warned the train crew not to fol
low them, and disappeared in the dark
ness.


A half hour after the hold-up, two
daughter of James Wayment, of War
rem, near by, were held I'D by two mer
who are suspected Of being the two
robbers who held up the Overland. The
girls were SO frightened and the nigh
was so dark that the young womer
could not give a definite description Of
the men. They declared one was shor
and the other tall, and passengers or
the train say this description in gen
eral way answers that of the men wh(
held up the Overland.

HERE are two ways of doing arithmetic and two
sorts of examples to do. Some people do sort,
some the other.


There are those who add plants to the gardens
before their doors no comforts to the houses
where they dwell new ideas to the business
at which they labor
Who by their pessimism subtract from the courage
of their friends and by their lack Of interest in
the common veal subtract from the beauty
and ideaIity of the community life
Who multiply causes Of dissension between acquant
ances, causes Of friction between employers and
employees, causes of strife in families and causes
Of failure in those too closely associated with
them.


Who divide nothing Of their but their anxietes.
doubts and fears, sharing these freely that others
may worry and doubt and fear with them.
There those who give but fractional part of the
love and service they owe.


AND


There are those who add fair flowers and luscious
fruit to their own gardens and the gardens Of
their neighbors, who, aided by sun and rain,
create pleasure for every passerby who make
homes out of houses in which they live, leaving
them more beautiful than when they found them;
who bring a new spirit of intelligence and power
into every business at which they labor. -
Those who, by their optimism, subtract from the
weakness or their friends ana take away from une
community life only those elements that make for
sickness, stupidity, evil, ugliness and death.
Who multiply reasons for loyalty and good faith in
the home and the Office the school and the church,
joining hands in friendship that are already near
enough together and forming partnerships founded
on integrity.


Who ready to divide their enthusiasm with you,
to share their courage and their life as well as
their books, their flowers and their dinners.
And there are those who are always striving to push
the decimal point to the right past the place
where they must stop giving.

FORT WORTH, Tex, March 3.-For
the first time in many years a woman
charged with murder IN the first degree
is to be placed on trial in this city next
Monday. The defendant in the case is
Mrs. T. NJ. Brooks, wife OF prominent
attorney, and her trial on the charge Of
having shot and killed Mrs. Mary Bin
ford, department manager OF a local dry
goods store, is to begin next Monday in
the Sixty-seventh district court.


The crime with which Mrs. Brooks Is
charged was committed on January 16
of this year and is believed to have been
prompted by jealousy. Neither Mrs
Brooks nor her husband has shown
any inclination to make a statement
that would indicate the cause of the
tragedy, but for some time there have
been rumors strongly limiting that Mrs.
Brooks did not live happily with her
husband and that she believed her hus-
bands affection had been alienated by
Mrs. Binford, who was divorced about
two years ago and was considered
rather fascinating and handsome wom-
an. 1t is expected that at the coming
trial some light will be thrown upon
the relations between the defendant and
her husband and between the latter and
the victim of the tragedy and this pros
pect has greatly intensified the public
interest in the case.


Armed with a revolver, Mrs. Brooks,
on the afternoon of January 16 made
her way to the dry goods store where
Mrs. Binford was employed, and as the
latter approached, Mrs. Brooks, without
saying a single word or giving any
warming, pulled her big revolver from
her mum. Mrs Binford, realizing her
danger, grappled with Mrs. Brooks and
tried to wrest the weapon from her.
Her strength was no match, however,
for that of Mrs. Brooks, and the latter
quickly freed herself and forced the
other woman against the wall. In the
scuffe the weapon was discharged, the
bullet plowing its way through Mrs.
Binford's hand.


With her victim at bay, Mrs. Brooks
stepped back and fired four times. The
second ball struck Mrs. Blnford in the
left shoulder. the third, one inch higher,
and the fourth entered the base OF the
neck, shattering the spinal vertebra.
Just before her victim sank to the
floor, Mrs. Brooks fired again, the bull
let striking Mrs. Binford behind the ear,
coming out through the top Of the head.


Mrs. Brooks was arrested and after
waving a preliminary trial, was re-
leased under $4,000 bail.

ing. So they hid everything that was OF
any value. The soldiers went by; only a
few soldiers stopped for drink. and then
went on. After all had gone there came
in sight a poor. lone soldier, staggering
under his burden. for he was hardly six
teen. and was very weak. He dropped to
the side of the road. gasping for water.
Shall we take him in" asked Ben. sure
w." said brave Elsie. They tended this
English soldier until he was We'll and

ceived parcel from him. In which they

Toronto, ont.-In the Porcupine dis
trict the loss of life from fires is
known to be several hundred and the
property loss will reach several mil
lion dollars


Only three of the eighty-four en-
ployes of the West Dome mine have
been accounted for and 200 miners,
muckers, etc, in the Dome mine have
been suffocated.


The mines burned include the Dome,
North Dome, Preston, East Dome,
Vipond, Foley OBrien, Philadelphia,
United Porcupine, Standard Imperial,
West Dome and Success.


Among the dead are Robert Weiss,
manager of the West Dome. and mis-
wife and child.


The Philadelphia mines loss is
about $4,000; United Porcupine's loss,
10000; Eldorado Porcupine, all build
ings destroyed; Standard, about s40,-
600; Imperial about $35,O00; Success,
probably destroyed; West mines,
about $4,000.


All reports give but a vague idea
of the loss of life and property in Por-
cupine camp, which probably will total
millions of dollars and hundreds of
lives.


In four short hours the fire swept
from the Standard mines through to
the shores of Porcupine lake, where
1t destroyed South Porcupine, Potts
vile and part of Golden City, as well
as many small buildings along the
lake front.


There the entrapped miners, cut of
from escape, were forced to take to
the shafts for safety and. penned in
by flames, perished. This was notably
true at Dome and West Dome mines.
At the Preston, East Dome, an untim-
bered shaft gave shelter and none per-
ished.


The streets of South Porcupine are
strewn with dead persons, horses.
dogs and cattle.


Along the mine roads are the
charred bodies of those overcome try
ing to escape.


OF the staff Of 300 at the Dome, but
.
Dome but three out of eighty-four en-
ployes are known to be alive. Along
the highway between East Dome ana
South Porcupine, over comparatively
open section, were found six charred
bodies.


The miners saw dense clouds OF
smoke to the southwest, where the
fires were raging. They gave little
heed. Later a small blaze started in
Lake View, of the Porcupine townsite,
but it passed almost unnoticed because
of the recent frequency of bush fires.


The dense smoke clouds began TO
roll over the Porcupine district. Then
the miners became alarmed and the
camps took on unusual activity. Mes
sengers were sent out and soon re-
turned with warnings that the fire was
travelling through the forest at rapid
speed and was licking up many town
ships.


Soon the fire had covered an area
of twenty-five miles in length and two
miles in width and was licking up the
base line of Tisdale, sweeping over the
Standard and Imperial mines at De-
lore, the Philadelphia, Shaw, Eldorado
and United Mines in southern Whit
ney.


Hundreds fled before the flames, but
the dense clouds of smoke hung low
over the land and made progress diff
cult. Many fell exhausted before the
fire as it swept over South Porcupine
The frame buildings burned fiercely.


Twenty minutes after the flames
struck the outskirts the town was in
ruins. All who escaped the flames
made for the water. where all sorts OF
water craft-launches, canoes. scows
and skiffs-were pressed into service.


Women and children were first hur'
ried into the small boats and started
off for Pottsville and Golden City.
where they were temporarily safe from
the flames.

PARA, Brazil, Jan. 5.-This city is an
armed camp today with machine guns
planted in the streets and the plazas
filed with the temporary Contonment
of regular soldiers who have been or
dered here to quell a revolutionary
outbreak.


Five are dead and at least fifty are
wounded as the result of regiment OF
cavalry charging mob in the streets
late yesterday, dispensing them with
volleys from their Carbines and the
vigorous use of their sabers. Additional
troops were rushed from Rio Janeiro
today and heavy guards were placed
about the federal buildings, and rapid
fire guns placed upon the roofs.


Several Brazilian men-of=war lie in
the harbor and the crews today threat
ened to take sides with the revolution
lists and shell the city. Foreign mer-
chantmen fearing that this threat would
be put into effect, weighed anchor and
left the harbor.


Business is practically dead, and the
authorities posted a proclamation de-
claring the city temporarily under mar
ttal law.

Little Aschsah Petty, eight years old,

outskirts of the city. The story so
timIdly told by the little girl, as she
stood at the knee of Judge Pugh, in
United States side of Police Court,
brought a sentence of year in Jail for
Gayer. Assault was the charge against
him.


The little girl. with light hair just
beginning to touch her shoulders, with
fair skin and blue eyes, modest and
timid, Won the hearts of everyone in
the court room as she told her story
to Judge Pugh.


Other witnesses, who rescued the
child from Gayer, were called. But the
child herself was her own best wit
ness.


Gayer took the girl out on Rhode
Island avenue and she was rescued
from him at the culvert where the
Baltimore and Ohio railroad tracks
cross the avenue.


Little Aschsah showed the effects of
the terrible nervous strain that she was
under during her carrying away and the
attack upon her. Her eyes were still
reddened from crying.


THE best little witness and the
bravest little girl that has come before
this court in years." were the words
spoken by judge and court officials after
the child finished her story.

PRINCETON. n. J., Oct. 2.-The past
weeks football practice at Princeton
has seen the start of the training table
which began on Wednesday with the
following fifteen men: Captain Hart,
Sawyer, Mccormick, Mclean, Winants
and White. seniors; Bluethenthal. Dun
lap, Penfeld, Pendleton, Wight and
Wilson, juniors; and Baker, De Witt,
and Vaughn, sopohmores.


The past week has been the first full
week of scrimmage, but the work as a
whole has been far from encouraging
The offensive work in particular has
been noticeably week, due in great part
to the inability of the line to afford
the backs any sort of interference. The
forwards are slow in getting started
and fail to get into the plays with the
proper spirit. This defect Is even more
noticeable when the varsity has the
ball near the scrubs goal line, and
when direct plunging would be most
profitable the line men are unable to
do their share Of the work.


This unexpected weakness may prove
especially costly for the Orange and
Black this year, as the backs are light
even for the Tigers, and without a
make headway against the heavier elev-
ems, such as Harvard and Yale.
Princeton has not had a line plunging
back Of first-rate caliber since the days
of Jim Mccormick. back In 1907. and
the efficiency of an eleven this year Is
largely dependent upon the possession
Of a heavy backfield man who not only
can hit the line hard, but can throw
off tacklers and keep going.
