BALTIMORE. July n.-Cheered by
about fifty rural admirers, Charles X.
Hamilton and Harry NJ. Atwood, the
daring Boston aviators. gracefully as
cended from small knoll on the west
end Of Walter r. Townsend's estate at
temmers Run, Nd. at ABS o'clock this
morning. and made magnificent start
for College Park, on the last lap of a
record-breaking overland flight from Bos-
ton to the National Capital.


The weather conditions could not have
been better. The sun had just peeped
above the eastern horizon. and the light
southwest winds fairly carried them fro..l
the ground at the first turn of the motor.
Ascending to an elevation Of about oOJ
feet, the aviators SKINNED gracefully
over the little group Of spectators, and
with q farewell wave headed to the
southwest and in a few seconds disap-
peared from view over the wooded hills.


Both the men and the machine were IN
excellent working condition. and thers
was not the slightest hitch. After five
hours Of restful sleep Hamilton and At
wood arose about 3:45 O'Clock and after
breakfast they went Into the field and
prepared for the flight.


Pass Over Fort McHenry.


A rigid examination was made OF the
motor and planes. the biplane was towed
to the top of the hill. the tank filled
with gasoline and the start made. The
PENNSYLVANIA railroad tracks were fol-
lowed to Bay View Junction. then chang
ing the course a little more to the west
ward the aviators few over the southern
and eastern outskirts of the city. pass
ing over historic Fort McHenry at ass
a. M. covering a distance Of nearly twelve
miles in half an hour.


More than two hundred soldiers sta
toned at the fort who had received word
beforehand that Atwood and Hamilton
intended to pass over the historic ram
parts were ready to greet them.


Soldiers Fire Salute.


They assembled on the parade ground
and when the aeroplane whizzed over
their heads they fired salute. Time did
not permit the aviators to circle the
fort but in return to the soldiers salute
they waved their handkerchiefs.


Leaving Fort McHenry, Atwood. who
was steering, headed the machine toward
the Patapsco and followed the river.
passing over Helethorpe aviation field
at 5:07 am


Again taking up the Pennsylvania rail-
road tracks at this point the pace was
and the distance of about
twenty-five miles between the two avia-
ton fields was covered In thirty-eight
minutes.

guns on stronger sloop and'put

willy stratagem he separated

NEW YORK, August 31.-Ten seamen
snatched from death in the great storm
that battered the south Atlantic coast
were brought here today by the Clyde
line steamer Mohawk. Last Tuesday
morning the Mohawk rescued them from
the crumbling hulk of the schooner NAL
colin B. Seavey, while the sea was
pounding their ship to pieces on a reef
of Georgetown, 8. c. News OF the res
cue came yesterday in a wireless dis
patch.


Originally there were eleven Of the
schooner's crew, from Bath. Me. The
man who lost his life during the forty
eight-hour struggle aboard the wave
swept schooner was q Portuguese sailor
known to his mates only as Tony. He
was swept overheard when the ship first
hit the sandbar last Saturday night.


Captain Almost Helpless.


The rescued men are Capt. Henry NJ.
Dodge. Mate s. S. Southard, Second Mate
Charles Norton. a. steward, an engineer
and five sailors. Capt. Dodge was almost
helpless from the battering he received
while clinging to spar. but the Other
nine men had almost recovered from their
cApcTiSHSc. lucy VIII icoSO w
day for Bath


The Seavey put out from Tampa. Fla,
on August 16 loaded with phosphate.
Saturday night she ran into the storm
and dropped anchor off Cape Roman.
BY Sunday evening the sea was sweep
ing over the schooner, opening her seams
and washing clean her decks. She drag
ged her anchors and began to pound on
the sandy bottom.


Took Refuge in Rigging.


The crew took refuge in the rigging
and by Monday morning the schooner be-
gan breaking up. Tuesday morning
after theree ships had passed in the dis
tance without observing her signals of
distress. the Mohawk appeared.


The rescue was as thrilling as the
plight of the schooner's crew. A boat
from the steamer could not get nearer
the Seayey than fifty yeards, and one by
one the exhausted men lashed to what
was left of the schooner's rigging, un-
tied the ropes and threw themselves into
the sea, and were hauled aboard the
small boat by lines thrown to them as
they struggled in the tremendous waves.

some hardship and suffering, accord

Newburg, n. Y, Jan. THE difficulty IN
the construction of the aqueduct for the
New York water supply tunnel under the
Hudson River between Cornwall and Storm
King, through which the water Is 10 flow
when the project is completed, has been
solved. For several years the engineers
have by drilling endeavored to find solid
rock at the bottom OF the river. A series
Of experiments, long continued and very
expensive revealed the fact that instead
of the bed OF the river being solid rock, 1t
was composed OF huge pieces Of stone,
which seemingly ages ago had broken OF
from the great mountains on either side
and fallen into the crevasse through which
the Hudson River now flows. There have
been times even when the plan OF tunnel
ling was almost abandoned because re-
peated experiments only disclo--. these
immense chunks of rock, ins ean OF the
solid rock which was sought


Success has now crowned the expert
nents after drilling laterally and perpen-
dlcularly. The shaft which was sunk on
the east side OF the river near Storm King.
between the New York Central Railroad
tracks and the river was put down l,lS0
feet, and the contractors have begun 70
tunnel westward toward the Cornwall
shore. Already the tunnel has been pushed
thirty feet, and the work Of carrying II
to the west side Of the river will be hast
ened without interruption.

A series Of petty thefts among nurses
at the Washington Asylum Hospital came
to a climax yesterday, when one of their
number. under cross-examination, con-
fessed that she was the guilty one.


For several weeks valuables and loose
change had been disappearing from the
nurses quarters. and at first the en-
ployes were suspected, but this suspicion
proved unfounded Gradually the sums
of money lost became larger. Miss
Bertha Bruchlacher missed several dollar
Ellis from her purse, and Miss Harriet
Sutton was later robbed of $3.50. Next,
Miss Gertrude Foote was relieved OF
$3.50, and another nurse of the contents
of Christmas box sent from her home.


When Miss Adelaide Parsons, the su-
perintendent OF nurses, received the re-
port that S24 had been stolen from Miss
Lizzie Cusack, the hospital cook, whose
room is on the same floor with several
of the nurses. she decided that the time
had come for an investigation. She was
confirmed in this opinion by discovering,
when she opened her desk, that same
morning, that $50 Of her money was
missing.


Detective Armstrong, of the Central
ofice, made an investigation. The re-
suit of his findings narrowed the field
down to a single nurse, and she was put
through cross-examination. Finally
she broke down and confessed that ever
since she could remember she had been
a kleptomaniac. She had spent none Of
the stolen money and had not used any
of the property. so no charge was pre-
ferred against her.


The guilty nurses name was not given
out by the hospital authorities. Her
resignation was accepted, and she left
the institution last night.

LONDON, October 1.-THE London
Daily Telegraph's war correspondent
sends this dispatch to his paper from
Tripo, describing the Turkish attack on
the forts at 2 o'clock Tuesday morning:


The Italians have won their first land
battle in fine shape. The friendly Arabs
gave the Italians warning Of the probable
attack by the Turks. They said that the
Turks would, no doubt, attempt to enter
Tripoli at night.


Ample precautions were taken to REIN
force the posts, particularly the new
works to the south.


The warships were about four miles OFF,
shore. The Turks were discovered about
l o'clock in the morning advancing in two
columns, supported by field guns. For
tunately, it was bright, moonlight
night, and the Italians ashore were jul
diciously assisted by searchlights.


All night the Turks approached Tripoli
in good order. There were thousands.
supported by native auxiliaries. When
they were within few hundred yards
the marines from the works and trenches
poured into their ranks tremendous
rife fire. supported by machine guns and
field artillery.


The intended Turkish surprise entirely
failed, but the Ottomans stood to the at
tack courageously, replying to the In
trenched Italians with heavy fire and
striving to press home the action, first
on the west. The Italian marines, how
ever, were not shaken


They were undaunted and fought most
brilliantly, firing with steady and deadly
accuracy They beat back every attempt
of the enemy. From 80 to am the
rifle fire was fierce. After that it dwindled
and ceased. The enemy retreated with
severe losses.


Behavior of Marines Admirable.


On the eastern side the attacking col
umn of Turks tried to turn that flank of
the Italian defense. They advanced into
the palm belt and threw shrapnel, which
fell near the sea. The Italians held fast
and drove away every advance on the
front flank.


The behavior of the sturdy marines was
admirable. 1t could not have been better
among any troops.


The fleet, cleverly arranged. contrib
uted TO the success of the battle. When
the rifle fire ecame heavy several yes
sells including the cruisers and battle
ships, opened with their minor batteries,
directing their shells over the town, SO
that they might fall among the Turks
and cover the Italian front TANKS against
rushes enmasse The firing of the fleet
was deliberate and well placed, and was
directed by signals and wireless After
the rifle fire had ceased the ships contin-
ued to pursue the retreating foe with
shells from their heavier batteries, in
GLIDING the six-inch and twelve-inch guns.
The firing continued until am. The
Italian casualties were slight.
People in Tripoli remained indoors and
were confident of Italian victory.

NRADE conditions are 30 advanced and


diversified in the United States and


Europe that 1t is dificult to realize the


fact that there are still some countries


where work Is carried on In primitive
way. But there are many countries where
trade 10 still carried on in a crude way and
where most Of tile work Is done by women.


This Is especially true OF Africa. Even in
those parts that have come in contact with
European influence the hardest work is
usually reserved for the women. Among the
negroes OF Guinea they perform most Of the
manual labor. Nearly every man has several
wives working for him. The women hoe the
gardens. carry great burdens on their heads
and paddle canoes.


At Kumassi nearly all the trading Is done
by women. Some work in the fields from early
until late. Others go to the market, where
they sell medicines, fuel, and primitive
kitchen utensils. When they are not barter
ing they are in the field planting maize and
yams. The men hunt game; they snare birds.
trap hsh, and make pits for the elephants
Both men and women carry the vegetables
and other goods to the market, but the men
are careful to return home early before the
great heat comes on.


Even lazier are the Hottentots of South
Africa. The men do absolutely no work ex-
cepr u care for the cattle and hunt. The
women do a great deal more than look after
their homes and children and work in the
fields They make straw baskets, mats, and
utensils, which they sell in the market There
are some smiths tanners, and tailors among
the men, and they trade among themselves
for cattle and armor which they make.

Estes to draw her allowance OF $50

land In the Fort Simcoe reservation

Josephine lived at Cello until a
vear ago. when she came to live with
her nephew, Charlie Quempts, whose
sewing machine, graphophone and
bread mixer mark his family as the
most advanced In the valley.


Some time ago she heard that her
ahack at Cello had been robbed, and

pulled out can containing gold,

and buried.

charitable persons in various cities are

aster.

When the cool morning comes along

search for clear complexion and general
radiance in long early-morning walks.

will add its quota to the inspiration or
the walk and bar all but happy thoughts
from the mind. Swing along at me-
diam gait. head erect, shoulders back.
ball of foot put squarely to the ground
and limbs swinging from the hips rather
than the knees Breathe deeply, being
careful to expel all the air from the lungs
after each breath, an operation which re-
quires rather loose garments. Above all.
don't forget the happy thought. Roses
for the cheeks and energy for the day
can be gathered at will during these
beauty walks.

Not only is the blood the great
nourishing source of our systems, but
equally as important is its work of
removing the waste of oxidized it's
sues which have been consumed in
force and bodily heat. This waste is
filtered out through the kidneys.
When, however, the kidneys become
weak and unable to perform their
regular duties, the waste is allowed
to remain in the circulation. soon
forming uric acid, which destroys the
greater portion of nourishing ele-
ments of the blood and leaves it weak
and acrid. This imperfect blood de-
posts into the different muscles and
joints the uratic impurity with which
it is contaminated. Then the pains
and aches of Rheumatism commence.
The gritty formation which uric acid
causes collects in the joints, pro-
duces the aches and stiffness which
always accompany the disease. Like
wise the muscles are coated and lose
their elasticity, while the continual
irritation to the nerves produces
swelling and inflammation of the flesh.

Fishing in the big irrigation districts
adjacent to Garden City without hook or
line is the newest diversion among men
and boys. Go out north, west or north
west from town any fine morning and you
will encounter men and boys going to
or returning from the bitches with fish
in ample quantities.


The United States Sugar and Land
Company's monster reservoirs are now
being emptied into the bitches for the
beet and alfalfa crops Thus thousands
Of fish find their way through the head
gates and into the bitches. The bitches
are running almost bank full One place
where one ditch is flumed across another
the water goes tumbling like small cat
aract. and 1t isn't an uncommon sight to
see the fish jump in the air and splash
into the water.


Men who are running the bitches, culti-
vators of growing beets, workmen at the
various pumping plants and men and boys

or stand or kneel beside the banks and
draw out the fish with their hands Many

course: many buffalo-one man caught q

nurturinR of the new Republic disap-

ing the city, found 1t easy to get beyond

tary Of State. General Armstrong, an
other soldier of the Revolution, was
Secretary of War.


Fort Washington, planned by Major
L'Enfant earlier in the war Of 1872, was
rushed to completion, but there were no
land defenses, and the old fort was
useless.

Washington at the approach of the
British. The soldiers devastated but
little private property during the brief
occupancy.

News reached here last night of furi-

bull on one hand and a half dozen men
on the other. 1t happened near Keegle-
town.

turned upon William Sheets and Henry
Layman. Sheets was knocked down and
sustained severe bruises about the legs.
Layman made his escape. The bull then
cleared several fences and waded right
into Levi Getz, sturdy Rockingham
farmer, on his own land. In his desper-
ate situation Getz literally took the


bull by the horns and the shaking and
tossing that followed was strenuous,


but doubtless saved Getz's life. Getz
finally was hurled to the ground, and,
having lost his hold, he escaped over a
fence.


The animal then made for Getz's daugh-
ter. Mrs. Jacob Armentrout. who was car
rying a bucket Of water in one hand. A


wild race for fence followed. 1t was a
Garrison finish for the woman. though
she dropped her bucket at the start. As
the excitement increased the crowd
swelled to a half dozen men and four
dogs.


The animal made nine stands in his
fight. but finally was compelled to retreat
to the big road in the face Of the furious
bombardment with stones and sticks that
followed.

Postmaster Merritt, after several
weeks of experimenting. announced this
afternoon that he will hereafter be able
to give the citizens of the District a
vastly improved special delivery service.


Under the law which created the spe-
cial delivery system the quick delivery
OF letters is all that Is provided for.
and that from the time the letters
reach the post ofice Of their address.
Postmaster Merritt's new plan goes
much farther, and extends to letters
mailed locally for special delivery.


The District has been divided into six
zones radiating from the general post
office and one mile in diameter. Letters
bearing special delivery stamps which
are deposited in the main Office for
local delivery will be sent out for de-
livery without any delay at all. beyond
what is necessary to properly prepare
them.

Italians have suffered their worst re-
I verse since the war with Turkey began.
according to news received here from
across the frontier. A body of italian
marines who started inland from Tripoli
encountered an overwhelming force of
Turks and Arabs and were driven back
to the city.

miles without seeing any sign of the
enemy. Suddenly the Turks and Arabs

foothills. The Italians were greatly

One weary mother who had let out
tucks in her small daughters petticoats
until she reached the stage Of rebellion
evolved this very simple and eficacious
plan OF lengthening: The shoulder seams
were made several inches longer than
was necessary. and instead of being
sewn together they were left open and
neatly bound around the edge with tape.
The petticoat was adjusted to the little
lady and the ends Of the shoulder seams
Tapped and fastened with the patent
clamps (such as hold the packets of
skirts). As she grew the laps became
smaller. until the full reserve was used.
This method makes easier work for the
laundress. too, as the little garments are
much more easier to iron with the
shoulder seams free.

John Devone were taken to their homes
in Absecon last evening unable to speak
from hoarseness and with their bodies
and faces swollen and burning after hav-
ing been attacked by swarms of mosqui-
toes and green flies.

island in the Absecon river. They had
taken off their clothes and were wading
in the water when they discovered that

gone. Each accused the other of playing
a practical joke, but it developed that the
rising tide had carried the boat out

shouted until they could no longer raise
their voices. There was no match with
which to start a signal fire that might
he seen on the mainland.


AS the mosquitoes and flies became
worse the men plunged into the water.
but the salt only made the pain worse. !.


When rescued the men were exhausted.
On their arrival home they were treated
by physicians.

The North German Lloyd liner Prinz
Friedrich Wilhelm and the Hamburg
American liner Kaserin Auguste Victoria
finished a neck and neck race clear across
the Atlantic when they arrived off the
Hook Monday evening. The Prinz beat
the Kaiserin by an hour and quarter
after giving her a handicap Of two hours
start from Cherbourg. Both boats docked
yesterday morning.


The feature Of the race was the storm
which the rivals encountered Thursday
the day the Prinz overhauled the Kaiserin
Herr Elsner, navigating officer of the
Prinz, said yesterday the wind was blow
ing eighty-five miles an hour and the waves
measured fifty-five feet from trough TO
crest. Both boats were smothertng their
bows and each looked TO the other as If
making the fight Of her life. From that
time on the two were never out Of sight Of
each other until Monday afternoon, when
a snow storm came between them.


The Prinz's time was eight days three
hours and eight minutes and her average
speed 1853 knots. Normally she makes
between eighteen and nineteen knots. This
is the first instance Of transatlantic race
between steamships in such storm.

SAN FRANCISCO, Jan. 6.-Three

contain letters and valuables worth
$4,000, have been stolen from mail wag-
ons somewhere between San Francisco
and Oakland, according to an announce
ment by the postal authorities today.


The robbery is baffling, as the bags
disappeared while being transferred by
ferry across the bay. The first was
taken December q; the second Decem-
Der q; and the third December g.


Postal authorities are seeking a check
of the missing bags, and they declare
that the fact that only bags contain
ing the largest amounts of money were
taken indicates that the thieves were
intimately acquainted with the post
office system here.

MERIDIAN. Miss. October .S.-Ruling
IN a damage suit involving the federal
employers liability act TO-DAY, State CIR
cult Judge Buckley held that if the cars
causing the accident carried interstate
shipments the state was without jurisdic-
ton. The Plaintiffs will attempt to show
that the cars did not carry interstate
matter.


W. l.. Cook. switching foreman, was
crushed between cars while making a
coup ing last May. He died. Cook 5
brothers and sisters brought suit for So,
coo against the Mobile and Ohio railroad.


Railroad attorneys replied by pleading
that the cars between which Cook was
crushed carried interstate freight and as
sorting that the remedy. if any, should
be sought in the federal courts

sert the cars were not carrying interstate
freight, and the trial, which will begin
November 3 here, will center this
point.

ried to the United States Supreme court.

this phase of the act in question has been
so construed.

Quincy, Mass, Aug. 26.-Surpassing in
size any Dreadnought of the world pow
ers now afioat, the battle ship Rivadavia,
built and equipped entirely by Americans
for the Argentine Republic, was launched
to-day at the yards Of the Fore River
Shipbuilding Company.


Just before the Rivadavia plunged into
the bay, Tom Sopwith, the English air
man, flew out from the Harvard avia-
ton field and circled around her gigantic
hull. Thus the two most potent factors
in modern warfare met.


A distinguished gathering of South
American diplomats and official repre-
sentatives of the United States and Eu-
ropean nations was on the deck of the
huge fighting craft when she slid into
the water. She was christened by Sonora
de Naon, wife of the Argentine Minister
to the United States, who represented
Sonora Saenz Pena, wife of the President
of the Argentine Republic.


The launching was the most Exclusive
event of the kind in recent years. Only
those summoned by special invitation
were permitted to be present. The official
guests arrived aboard a special train
from Boston.


A peculiar sort of mixed pride in this
new sea monster was felt by Americans
who witnessed the ceremonies. The Riva-
davia was designed by American en-
gineers, built solely by American work.
men. and will be fitted from stem to
stern and masts to keelson by Ameri-
cans.


The Fore River Shipbuilding Company,
at whose yards the launching took place,
built the hull of the vessel under con-
tract, and the Bethlehem Steel Com
pany made the armor plate. The Bethle-
hem company will also construct the big
guns, which. when put in place, will give
the Rivadavia the most powerful broad
side of any vessel that ever sailed the
seas.


In displacement, the true measure Of
size. the Rivadavia exceeds the largest
vessels of the American navy, and also
the Hercules. Colossus, and Lion, the
great English Dreadnoughts now being
built

mile and half below Ossining, they saw
a train approaching on the track between
whose rails they were walking. The boy
and the girl crossed to the track nearer
the river and continued their walk and
talk.


But the behavior Of those in the engine
cab Of the train which they had just
avoided was very puzzling to the two.
The whistle sounded constantly, and the
fireman stood swaying in the forward
side door of the cab as with his hands
and arms he made emphatic motions.


Wondering, the two stood still for a
moment. Then a rapidly increasing roar
behind them made the boy turn around
Almost upon them was an express rush
ing at full speed. If young Kingsley had
wavered before, he did not now. With a
movement that was far quicker than the
firemans frantic gestures, he seized the
girl by the arm and. lifting her from the
roadbed. sent her spinning down toward
the Hudson. The girl toppled toward the
water. She stopped herself with an effort
just as her feet touched the water.


Then. safe herself she looked about for
the boy. He lay in a heap beside the rail-
road track. There had not been time for
him to jump. The train had struck him
He was reported last night dying in the
Ossining Hospital from a fractured skull
An arm was also broken. Miss Avery

For the first time in the history of the

opy held by four of the bridegroom's

fingers as he spoke them, n deep hush
fell over the assembly. From the in
tense faces OF the spectators they seemed
e. be striving to assist the young couple

The faces of TIE bride and bridegroom,

moment they took their places before the
rabbi until at the end of the ceremony

When the benediction had been pro-

guage, the bride, for the first time since
entering the temple raised her veil, re-

After the ceremony Mr.. and Mrs. Plap-

The Olympic sailed from Southampton

way of Cherbourg and Queenstown. She
sailed with the largest list of first-class
passengers that ever started across the
Atlantic on one ship. The first cabin
passengers number 742, twenty-four more
than her best previous record. Among
them were between twenty and thirty
American millionalres. and something like
$4,000 had been paid in passage money.

on board


The accident was an extraordinary one
Both ships were steaming in the same
direction, when the Hawke, IL is claimed.
ran stem on into the liner. tearing a large
hole in the latters starboard quarters.
both above and below the water line. The
Olympic's collision doors We're promptly
closed but the vessel made a good deal
of water. After a cursory examination of
the damage done the Olympic steamed
slowly back to Southampton. The Hawke
was so damaged in her bow that her col
lision mats were gotten out, but the
cruiser was able to proceed later unas-
sisted.


Naturally there was intense excitement
among the liners two thousand odd pas
sengers, but 1t was soon evident that
there was no cause for alarm.

September. When they had been here

that she loved Cecil, and him alone, q"
and that she would not live with her
husband any longer.

Miller suddenly left the city. Mr.. Huber
traced them to Chicago, Omaha, and
back again to Chicago, and finally to
Zion City, where Dowie hourished as a
prophet. The husband declares in his
petition that he has now lost all trace

wages, walked out. More men are now
out than any other time since the strike
was called.

sympathetic strike, which will go into
effect Wednesday IL 1t Is decided upon

the prolonged non-settlement will re-
suit in a general strike throughout
England. that will close most of the
ports.

the mems demands are experiencing
little difficulty. but all others are
badly hampered and in many instances
have had to suspend.

companies have yielded, shipping is

The handsome country residence
known as Penn-Dennis at Munsons
Hill. near Falls Church. Va. and owned
by Mrs. Louise Hillard Patterson of
1I75 California street was burned to
the ground Wednesday night. There
was a small insurance.


This house was one Of the landmarks
of the county. The main part was built
sixty years ago by Mr. Munson. and
the uprights and beams were of hewn
oak. eight inches by eight inches. The
house was hundred feet long by
fifty-two feet wide. containing seven
teen rooms. Large porches twelve feet
wide surround the house.


Mrs. Patterson and her daughter, who
had been in Washington during the day,
were sitting at the dinner table when
the dogs commenced a vigorous bark
ing. Mrs. Patterson went to the door
to see what was the matter and saw
a blaze OF light. A moment later she
discovered one of the chimneys on fire,
the flames leaping from the chimney
many feet high. The family rushed out
and called for help. Much of the fur
niture was carried out of the lower part
of the house. but the flames spread
so rapidly that nothing was saved from
the second floor. Mrs. Patterson has
owned the place over twenty years and
had made many improvements.

that Charleston, S. c.. had been sub.

terrific hurricane that devastated that

only affected outlying islands.


According to the story told by pas
sengers, the city's lighting system was
cut of, all telephone and telegraph
wires blown down, and piers and
wharves destroyed. Islands off the
coast, they said, were completely sub
merged by an unprecedented rise In the
sea.

that the city had been greatly DANA ged
by the storm and high water. No lives
were lost

NEW YORK, Aug. 8.-Facing a heavy
sea and strong wind and with the
rain falling heavily, Miss Elaine Cold
ing Of Bath Beach. swan fifteen miles
yesterday and won the women's swim
ming race from the Battery TO Steeple-
chase Park, Coney Island She out
swan two other noted mermaids and
fourteen men, members of the United
states Life Saving Corps, who started
over practically the same course In
another race.


MISS Golding swan the distance in six
hours and one minute. Miss Lillian
Howard, of Brooklyn, who finished Sec
ond. completed the course about a half
hour later. Mrs. Clara Bouton. of
staten Island. the other contestant in
the Women's race, found the ordeal too
trying and quit before half the dis
tance had been covered


Miss Golding's feat was remarkable.
Seldom has the course over which the
race was held been rougher than 1t
was yesterday. The whitecaps rose
fully three feet and strong wind blew
In her face almost all the way. Prac-
tically all the time she was in the
water the rain fell in torrents. So bad
were the conditions that rowboats and
launches met with much difficulty in
covering the course


Rounding Norton's Point, the smaller
boats found it impossible TO travel, and
were compelled to ask assistance from
the launches. And while these boats
were being towed Miss Golding sped
through the water and finished fresh
and strong. At the end she made little
of the feat, but added that she had
swan her last long-distance race.


Il feel fine and dandy" she said as
she leaped from the surf and grabbed
her bathrobe. But never again for
me. The distance is too long. 1 like
long swims. but five miles is enough.
went into this race simply to prove
that / possess endurance as well as
speed. Now that / have proved this,
shall cunhne my swims to five miles
nr less"

Captain William II. Van Schaick. who
was in charge of the General Slocum when
she was burned in the East River few
years ago, with the loss of thousand
lives. was paroed by the United States
government yesterday. and left Sing Sing
prison, returning to his wife and fanny
in Manhattan.


He had served two years and half, was
one of the model convcts. and served as
captain Of the little boat Bristol. which
was used for carrying convicts and pro-
visions back and forth TO Bear Mountain
when that site was being prepared for the
new prison. But Bear Mountain was
abandoned when the new site further up
the river was decided upon, and since then
Van Schaick had been DOING odd Jobs
feeble to do any Of the hard work that
convicts are usually put 10.


The old captains eyesight has been bad
within the last year. and this was another
reason that he had been assigned to the
comparatively light work about the flower
beds and greenhouses.


1t was known that the officials al Wash
ington had been appealed TO TO parole the
old captain. but the arrival of the parole
papers to-day was a surprise. apparently,
to the aged convict. and he was nearly
overcome when the glad news was told
him by Warden Johnson.


He said this afternoon before leaving
the prison that he would go straight 10
Manhattan 10 his wife and family. but he
did not know what he would do after that.

il was predicted that the author would

the daughter Of a bookseller in the town
of Wellington whose name was Smith
The name which she used in private life
was that which appeared on the title pages
of her books, and the authorities differ
as to what her trYe name was. Halkett

a pseudonym for Sarah Smith. whereas

Hannah Smith. She was born in 1871,


She wrote for Charles Dickens from
1850 until his death Afterward she
wrote stories Of a religious and philan-
thropic trend which were translated into
all the European and several Asiatic
languages.


"fhe Travelling Post ONCE" appeared

Courtship," "The Doctors Dilemma"
Hester Morley's Promise" Half
Brothers." Garcia" "Jessicas First
Prayer" "Bede's Charity" "The Soul OF
Honor" and The Highway of Sorrow"

Without president or executive gov

threatening to fight for supremacy,

peace and order In Hayti.

President Simon more than two score
persons have been killed and many
wounded In street fighting. A com
mittee OF safety organized by the
diplomatic corps and having the sup

Antenor Firmin are both candidates
for the presidency. Each have large
following. Neither of the leaders as
yet has reached Port Au Prince.

open her eyes he dragged her from the
bed and choked> her. Miss Carabaugfl
pluckily fought back. using her teeth on
the thiefs face. For nearly half hour
she fought.

Carabaugh resorted to strategy. She
feigned unconsciousness, and the bur-
glar threw her on the bed and for min
ute held her throat to make sure she

threw her feet up and kicked the bur-
glar in the face with terrific force. With
a groan the intruder fell senseless to the
floor. Miss Carabaugh ran out and called
the police. but the burglar revived. jump
ed out the second-story window and
escaped.

hold OF her arm and tried to lead her

pleaded to be allowed to say a few
words to the jury. Judge Hosmer
noticed her, and, stopping court pro-
ceedings, granted her request.

LONDON. December 31.-During the
short week on the stock exchange, in
which the final settlement of the year
was arranged, business was somewhat
restricted, but the tone was good through
out and prices were generally higher.
Dealers are looking for an expansion
of business with the release Of dividends
next week. The chief business was again
in foreign bonds and home rails, with
interest broadening in Rhodesian mines
yesterday. but reacted today on poor
trade reports, and closed dull and a
point higher on the week. Money was
exceedingly scarce, owing to year-end
requirements, and the market borrowed
a huge amount from the Bank of Eng
land. This sum, however, will be re-
leased early in the new year, and with
the dividend disbursement, will make
conditions easier. although the recur-
renee of the foreign gold demand has
somewhat dampened the prospects for
extreme ease in rates


Money was scarce and dearer today.
Discount rates were inclined to weaken
in anticipation of cheaper monetary con-
ditions shortly.


The attendance was light on the stock
exchange and only small business was
done. COnsols hardened a fraction, but
kaffirs and copper shares declined on
realizing.


American securities started quietly
steady. but support was lacking and
prices eased off partially. The closing
was quiet with values a small fraction
either side Of parity.

The two-masted river schooner J. Stef-
fins, which arrived here yesterday with
lumber from the st. Marys river, had a
long and rough trip from the time she
left here. after discharging her cargo,
until she tied up at the 10th street
wharf. The vessel left here about the
middle of December. just before the first
freeze of the winter came, and went to
the St Marys river. where she loaded
lumber. The freeze caught her in the
st. Marys and kept her from moving for
several days. Finally she was. worked
out of that river and started up the Po-
tomac. She had reached Riverside, about
half way to this city, when the drift ice
caught her, and. being unable to get
tug to tow her to this city, her master
put her about and ran back to the st.
Marys for harbor. There she remained
until about ten days ago, when a start
was made for this port. Foul weather
again caught her and she was forced to
seek shelter in Upper Machodoc creek.
from which point she sailed for this
city a day or two ago.

Niagara Falls. July 25.-"Bobby" Leach
Is the second person to go over the
Horseshoe Falls Of Niagara and live to
tell the story. He made the trip this
afternoon while large crowds watched
the spectacle from both sides Of the
river.


Leach sent his barrel-boat of steel up
the river along the New York side yes
terday. and to-day he was taken from
Cayuga Creek. near La Sale, well out
In the Canadian channel. The launch
towed the barrel far down stream, and
II was not until the danger point for
boats had been reached that the barrel
was closed and Leach was set adrift.


Faster and faster the waters carried
him, and then 100 feet out from the
Canadian shore they dropped out from
under him and let him drop into the wa
ters of the gorge. where they boil and
toss in their maddened whiteness at the
foot of the watery fall.


The barrel went out Of sight A moan
went up from the watching humanity,
as thousands of eyes watched for the
appearance OF the barrel speck on the
waters that rush out from the down.

ports brought 461 steerage passengers,
mostly Italian immigrants, nine Of them
Ill. The ships surgeon reported tha-

their illness on the trip.

tients transferred to Swinburne Island.

meteorological examination that will not
be completed until tomorrow morning
will show definitely the naturs of the
ailments in the cases Of suspicious
type. The Oceania also has seventeen
first cabin and liz second cabin passen-
gers. The ship and all aboard Will be
detained for further examination.


The Italian steamship San Giorgto, in
to-day from the Mediterranean, brought
no passengers, except one stowaway, but
brought a very large and valuable cargo,
including Al, 400 boxes Of lemons, which
she did want detained; so she refused
passengers. The crew, however. will be
detained for a close inspection. DIR. Doty
said this evening that one member Of the
crew of he San Giorgio had symptoms
resembling those Of cholera, and this may
detain the ship, after all.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


CINCINNATI. December If there
was any set of ball players who hailed
the finish of the 1911 season with marked
exultation, that set was composed OF
pitchers They had a hard. tumultuous
time during the campaign, and they We're
glad to Sc winter approaching-an Off
season during which they could figure out
new ways to stop the batsmen and over
come the handicap of the 1911 schedule.
Taking it as a concrete proposition, the
1911 season gave the pitchers more wor-
ries than any year since the foul strike
rule was invented. Aided by a ball that
was quite a bit livelier than in bygone
days the batsmen cut loose, spanked the
general averages. They might have built
them UP still higher but for the out
fielders, who caught more flies than in
previous seasons. and were kept busy
yanking in the long drives that fell near
the fences. Happy was the hurler who
had good outfield artists In his train, for
they saved him many and many a bump
ing!


: The 1911 season. however. proved a
gold mine for certain pitchers, some OF
them previously considered Of but little
value. Men who had a jumping curve
that created many strike-outs were the
lucky children. The fellow who relied on
control and good support was in hot
water most Of the time, for the batters
banged them as they came across the
center, and the hits were so savage that

In her chin, her body was badly bruised,

laundering down from the 116th

London. Sept So.-Among the exhibits for
the new London Museum classified last
month was the historical costume collec-
ton which almost fell into the hands Of
the Metropolitan Museum. of New York.
This magnificent exhibit has for its nucleus
the splendid Seymour Lucas collection, for
which the authorities OF the American in
stitution had been negotiating. The series
comprises three or four hundred costumes
dating from the fourteenth century to the
present day.


Among the costumes are the coronation
robes OF five sovereigns-Queen Victoria,
Queen Alexandra. Queen Mary. King Ed
ward VII and George V. The Elizabethan
and Jacobean periods are marked by ex-
ouiste costumes. and the commonwealth
is recalled BY number of beautiful silver
embroidered leather coats.


The classifying is being done by Guy
Laking, the Kings armorer, at Kensington
Palace. I'm the room IN which queen Anne
died. II IS said that the Queen died from
smallpox, and the classifers are hoping
that all the germs have died from old age.
The centrepiece of the new museum, which
was the idea Of King George and for which
he has granted the use OF Kensinston Pal
ace, is part of a Roman galley. the only
remains of these ancient ships known 10
exist. The remains were found under sew
oral feet OF Thames mud when excavations
were made for the new County Council hall.
The timbers are of oak, which had swollen
Immensely from centuries Of immersion in
the mud. but which shrunk when exposed
10 the air. II is expected that the King
will open the museum in October.

Automobiles are bringing to Washing

has impressed Itself on Maryland. Dur

From the New York Times.


The fatal fire in the Carlton Hotel, Lon
don. causes establishment only because
such fires are rare in England. A COM
paratively low structure, and solidly built,
the Carlton has never been thought un-
safe. But buildings Of the most approved
modern type. pronounced fireproof by ex-
perts, are not safe abiding places when
fire RACES in some part Of them and dense
smoke fills their corridors. Compared
with the new Ritz, the Piccadilly and even
the rebuilt Claridge's, the Carlton was
an old-fasfioned structure. Its corridors
were many and narrow, Its exits few
and far apart. Inevitably, it was filled
with quick burning material. But few
hotels the world over have been con-
sidered safer. and certainly few If any
have been more capably managed. The
report that twenty-five minutes elapsed
between the alarm summoning the en-
gines and the playing of the first stream
of water on the ruins lacks verification.
II il is true, the wonder Is that the en-
tire building. which Includes His Majesty's
Theater, directed by Sir Herbert Tree,
was not laid in ruins. The London fire
department is neither slow nor inefficient.
but the alarm may have been delayed by
the hotel people, possessed by the mis-
taken idea that they could subdue the
flames themselves.

Colonial Beach, garbed in Its holiday
| attire, today is welcoming visitors from


Virginia. Maryland. and the. District
hundreds to view and participate in the
| celebrations attending colonial week"
which opened this morning.


The little summer colony at Washing
toms Atlantic City" never mas put up
day. With thousands OF wards of bunt-
ing, which wraps the little cottages
from basement to gable; with flags
of all nations furled TO the breezes,
and the boardwalk hlled with visitors
spirit prevails.


Colonial week." which will extend
through Thursday night, opened auspi-
ciously. A bright, warm sun, which
shot UP from across the Potomac this
morning. told the residents OF the re-
sort that they would be favored with
ideal weather. They took Up their work
, with renewed vigor. and by the time the
first launch came chug-chuggng down
the river with its half-dozen Washing
ton visitors, everything was ready fo-
their reception.


The real and formal opening, how
ever, will not occur till this afternoon.
This morning the visitors have been
shown over the town" and have Whiled
the hours by plunges in the river. This
afternoon the mayor of Colonial Beach,
the town CounCilmen, and the commit
tees in charge OF the affair Will gather
in the pavilion located over the salt
waters, and will formally open the three
days celebration. A score or more
boats from the Potomac Boat Club and
other clubs Of Washington were taken
to Colonial Beach yesterday afternoon,
and this afternoon will engage in one
of the most spirited water contests ever
seen there.


Extra boats have been required in car
rying the crowds from Washington to
the beach. Charles ST. John. president
of the Potomac and Chesapeake Steam
boat Company. said this morning that
his company will have little difficulty In
handling the crowds, however.

KEEL, Germany, January 1S.-The sink
ing Of the U.s." the German navy's first
submarine disaster. cost three lives.


The dead are the captain of the sub
marine. and Lieuts. Fisher and Kobe,
the latter the helmsman. Their deaths
were due to an unforeseen mishap at the
moment that the officials Of the navy
were receiving congratulations upon the
supposed successful raising Of the "u-3''
and the rescue OF the crew.


When the submarine, three hours after
she sank. had been brought to the sur
face by the salvage ship vulkan yester-
day and twenty-seven Of her men had
made their way to safety through the
torpedo tube, the captain and the two
lieutenants elected to stand by their boat
until she was once more master of her.
self


The three men were in the coming
tower L. which remained submerged
when the vessel rose obliquely. Here the



for some time, as the boat had con.
siderable supply of oxygen, but for an
accident that shut of this supply from
the tower.


Oxygen Supply Cut OF.


Word was sent out that the raising had
been successful and that the crew was
safe. The work was continued, when
suddenly a ventilator gave way. permit
ting the water to rush into the subma-
rine. isolating the tower and cutting of
the oxygen upon which the three officers
were dependent. With the thrush Of
water the bow of the ship rose quickly.
but the stern. where the tower Il" is
located. sank deeper. Recognizing the
peril Of the officers, the rescuers worked
desperately to reach them, but it was
sixteen hours before an entrance to the
tower could be forced. Long before that
time the men had died OF suffocation..
They had failed to answer the signals of
had come hours before the bodies were
recovered.


With little hope, artificial respiration
was attempted. but the futility Of this
was soon evident.


Lieut.. Fischer was married week ago.


Hasty Judgment Blamed.


The loss Of the officers is peculiarly dis
tressing. as the fatalities are attributed
to too hasty attempt to raise the SUBJ
marine with a small crane before the ar
rival Of the more powerful Vulkan. The
crane lifted only the bow, and after twen-
ty-seven of the crew had made their es-
cape the small crane released the sub
marine to permit the Vulkan to operate.
\ rising sea complicated the subsequent
operations. which were conducted
throughout the night with the aid of a
searchlight. The heavy sea is held re-
sponsible for the giving way OF the ven-
tilator, the immediate cause OF the
tragedy.

BATAVIA, n. Y, Jan. 13.-Four per-
sons were killed and twenty injured, in
a rear-end collision on the New York
Central railroad here today. The wreck
caught fire.


The Buffalo SPECIAL was in the sta
tion discharging and taking on pas
sengers when the Western Express
crashed into it, telescoping two
Slecpers and a passenger coach.


The engine of the express turned
over and rolled 200 feet, emptying boil
ing water over the passengers who had
been hurled from the telescoped cars.
Two of the dead were found pinned
under the upset engine.


Rescue Is Difficult.


The fire in the ruins hindered the res
cuers. Batavia is not a scheduled stop
for the Boston Special, but the train
stopped to take on water. A heavy fog
prevailed which obscured the signals.
and this is believed to have been the
direct cause of the accident.


The trains were running about twenty
minutes apart Within a few minutes
after the accident twelve of the injured
who were found lying along the track,
were rushed to the Batavia hospital,
where it was said that a number OF
them were mortally hurt.


Nearly every physician in town was
hurried to the scene OF the wreck.
Trainmen expressed the belief that two
bodies lay under the wreck OF the
Western Express locomotive in the
ditch beside the tracks, and orders were
sent for a wrecking train to lift the
giant locomotive. The boiler of the
engine was punctured and boiling water
and Jets of scalding steam played upon
the wreckage.


Wreckage Piles on Engine.


Several were riding in the smoker on
the Western Express, which crumpled
up, the wreckage pilinG down upon the
PROSTATE locomotive which had been
hauling the train.


The impact was so great that the
forward cars Of the locomotive of the
BOSTON Special were derailed, but did
not turn over. All of the passengers
were badly shaken up.


Four cars which were telescoped were
reduced to fragments and pieces of them
streWn for hundreds of feet.


The railroad officials, who arrived half
an hour after the accident, made an in
vestigation, after which they declared
that the signals had been set correctly.
The opinion was expressed that the
Western Express was running ahead of
schedule.


Arriving with the railroad officials
came two W-recking trains and a special
train carrying doctors and nurses. The
Batavia fire department was summoned
to the scene and eXtinguished the fire
which had threatened to consume the
mass OF debris.
